title: What does healthy bushland actually look like?
standfirst: It looks messier than you think. The science behind bringing back the bush.
hero_alt: Bushland with fallen logs, leaf litter and a dense understorey beneath the trees
description: Researchers added 2,000 tonnes of dead wood to the ground at Mulligans Flat and found significantly more reptile species nine years later. Why structure, dead wood and hollows decide whether a planting ever becomes habitat.

flow.p: At the Mulligans Flat woodland experiment near Canberra, researchers added 2,000 tonnes of dead wood to the ground and waited.

Nine years later they counted significantly more reptile species than before. There was a clear dose response, so the more logs they had put down, the more lizards they found. And the effect was strongest exactly where the tree cover was thinnest.

This is awkward, because a healthy Australian bush looks, to most Australian eyes, like something that needs tidying up. Fallen timber. Leaf litter. Scrappy, prickly understorey. Almost every instinct we have about a well-kept landscape is wrong, and the science on this is not close.

It is National Science Week, and this year’s schools theme is Seeds of Science: Nurturing Knowledge for All, so it seems a good moment to say something we do not say loudly enough at the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife. Restoring the bush is not gardening at scale. It is applied science, it is harder than planting, and most of the difficulty sits in the parts nobody photographs.

blocks.heading: A bush is a building, not a lawn
blocks.alt: Fallen timber and leaf litter on the floor of healthy bushland
blocks.caption: The mess matters, and not for sentimental reasons.

flow.p: The mess matters, and not for sentimental reasons.

When Australian researchers compared remnant woodland against two kinds of revegetation, woodlots of trees alone and ecological plantings with trees, shrubs and understorey, bird richness tracked structural complexity. Floristic richness on its own showed no significant effect. At around twenty years both planting types had caught up to the remnants on raw species counts. The composition had not, and the remnants still held species that appeared in no planting at all.

More recent work using ground-based and drone LiDAR arrived at the same place from a different direction. The strongest predictors of bird abundance in a restored woodland were canopy roughness, vertical complexity in the ground layer, total vegetation volume and canopy height. The understorey, in other words. The layer satellites are worst at seeing, and the layer humans are quickest to remove.

A bush is not a surface with trees on it. It is a building with several floors, and the wildlife lives on all of them. Which is why NSW Government revegetation guidance recommends planting around 60 per cent shrubs, ideally dense and prickly, and keeping linear plantings at least 30 metres wide. Not a canopy. A structure.

blocks.heading: The floors you cannot rebuild
blocks.alt: An old eucalypt carrying the hollows that take more than a century to form
blocks.caption: Some of those floors can be re-established in a season.

flow.p: Some of those floors can be re-established in a season. Others cannot be re-established inside a working lifetime, and those are precisely the ones that look most like neglect.

Dead wood is the first. In 2003, the NSW Scientific Committee formally listed the removal of dead wood and dead trees as a Key Threatening Process, alongside feral cats and land clearing. Not a shame. A listed threat. The determination names the broad-headed snake, the regent parrot, the pink cockatoo and the spotted-tailed quoll among the species affected, and notes that stripping dead wood out alters the soil microclimate and starves the invertebrate communities doing the nutrient recycling. Research at Mulligans Flat found soil beside fallen logs gained measurable carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus within two years, concentrated in the top centimetre. A log is not debris. It is shelter, slow-release fertiliser, and a nursery for the fungi that everything above ground depends on.

The second is older again. In eucalypts, hollows suitable for wildlife take between 120 and 200 years to form, through branch loss, fungal decay, termite activity and weather. Around 300 Australian vertebrate species use them. That timeline cannot be shortened with funding and the result cannot be manufactured. The powerful owl nesting somewhere tonight is in a tree that was already old when Australia became a country.

Put those two together and you have the real asymmetry of this work. A tree can be planted this winter. The hollow in it will not be available to wildlife until the 2200s. Which is why protection is not the cautious half of conservation. It is the only way to hold onto the parts of the system that nobody can replace.

blocks.heading: What the soil remembers
blocks.alt: Ground layer plants and leaf litter over native soil
blocks.caption: If the oldest layers cannot be rebuilt, the question becomes what a landscape can still do for itself.

flow.p: If the oldest layers cannot be rebuilt, the question becomes what a landscape can still do for itself. Quite a lot, as it happens, by mechanisms stranger than most people expect.
Take a seed from many Australian natives and give it perfect soil, water, warmth and light. Nothing will happen. It will sit there, alive and refusing. What it is waiting for is smoke.

In 2004, chemists at the University of Western Australia isolated the compound in bushfire smoke that breaks seed dormancy. It works at concentrations as low as ten nanomolar. They named the family karrikins, after karrik, a Noongar word for smoke recorded in the Perth region in the 1830s. Australian plants are not passively waiting for rain. They are reading chemical signals in the soil, and much of the bush holds a store of dormant seed underground waiting for the right one.

But that store is a partial archive. In a study of eucalypt wetland forest at Yellingbo in Victoria, researchers germinated more than 6,300 seedlings from soil samples and found only about 24 per cent floristic similarity between the standing vegetation and what was held beneath it. Very few seeds of the wetland trees and shrubs were present at all. Exotic species made up 32 per cent of the standing vegetation but 41 per cent of the seed bank.

The soil remembers the ground layer. It remembers the weeds rather well. It does not reliably remember the canopy. That gap is exactly where the work sits, and it is why 145 living seedbanks and more than 30 community nurseries across four states sit inside our Fire Wise program, and why 110,000 fire-resilient natives have been propagated and planted rather than bought in from wherever was convenient.

flow.h: The question that comes before planting

flow.p: All of which leads to a single diagnostic question, and it is not the one most people expect.

Australia’s national restoration standards set out a principle that should govern far more conservation spending than it currently does: restoration inputs will be dictated by level of resilience and degradation. Translated, the first question on any site is never what shall we plant. It is whether this place can still repair itself, and if not, what exactly is broken.

Get that wrong and you can spend a decade planting into a landscape that will not take it. On the Cumberland Plain west of Sydney, eleven years after planting and with 71 per cent of planted species established, species composition at all three restored sites remained significantly different from reference woodland. Only five planted species had produced recruits of their own. In the Western Australian wheatbelt, soil organic carbon under trees planted a decade earlier sat at 0.9 per cent, against 1.2 to 1.5 per cent under reference woodland. The trees were there. The system had not come back with them.
Planting is the beginning of the process. It is not the proof of it.

blocks.heading: Distance is a habitat feature
blocks.alt: Bushland running unbroken across a wide landscape
blocks.caption: There is one more variable, and it has nothing to do with the site itself.

flow.p: There is one more variable, and it has nothing to do with the site itself. It is where the site sits.

A systematic review of 80 Australian connectivity studies found a mean gap-crossing distance of around 106 metres, and a threshold for dispersal between patches of around 1,100 metres. Those two numbers decide whether two patches of bush are one habitat or two. When the answer is two, the losses arrive slowly enough to be missed. Ecologists call it extinction debt: species still present in a fragment, still being counted in surveys, but no longer viable there. On the Swan Coastal Plain in Western Australia, banksia woodland patches were found to carry an average extinction debt of 13 species each, equivalent to 28 per cent of mean species richness. The bill had not been paid. It had only been deferred.

Scale is the counterweight. Research across Victorian farmland found landscapes with 1 per cent revegetation held an average of 11 woodland bird species. At 15 per cent revegetation, the average was 25.

This is why Growing National Parks is an ecological strategy and not merely a real estate one. Our 23,000-hectare acquisition at Undilla Station sits adjacent to Boodjamulla. Mundoo Island’s 1,900 hectares went into Coorong National Park rather than standing alone. We added 29,479 hectares to national park status across the last year, and the question we ask of every hectare is what it connects to.

blocks.heading: What a full bush actually means
blocks.alt: Bushland with a full canopy, midstorey and ground layer
blocks.caption: A bush with all of its floors, not just its canopy.

flow.p: All of it. The canopy, the midstorey, the prickly scrub, the litter, the logs on the ground and the fungal networks underneath. Gaps narrow enough to cross and patches large enough to hold. Old trees left standing long enough to go hollow.

We measure that against a local reference ecosystem using six attributes and a five-star scale, and we publish what it produces: 647 hectares under active restoration last year, 1,215,443 trees, shrubs and seedlings planted across priority landscapes, and 80 per cent delivery of purpose. Numbers we put in writing because they can be checked.
Growing National Parks, Saving Species and Healing the Land are three answers to one question, which is what does this particular landscape need, and in what order.
Australia looks better with a full bush. Not a tidy one.

title: A wildlife corridor is only as wide as its narrowest point
standfirst: Urban sprawl rarely wipes out a wildlife corridor outright. It pinches them: a subdivision here, a road widening there, a reserve that takes decades to fully secure. Australia is good at identifying the corridors that matter. The harder part, the part that decides whether a population holds on, is delivering them at the width, length and permanence that actually works. Four of the country’s fastest growing regions show what that gap looks like on the ground, and what closes it.
hero_alt: A koala crossing a road at the edge of a growing suburb
description: Urban sprawl rarely wipes out a wildlife corridor outright, it pinches it. Four of Australia's fastest growing regions show what width, continuity and permanence actually decide, from a chlamydia free koala population in south west Sydney to an overpass in Brisbane that has worked since 2004.

flow.p: At dusk in Sydney’s south-west, a koala comes down out of a grey box and starts moving. She is not lost. She is doing what her mother did, and her mother before her, following a route between habitat patches her population has used for generations. The difference is what now sits across that route: roads, fences, and the steady spread of the city. Her population is one of the most important koala populations in the country, and its future depends on whether those old routes stay open.

We count habitat loss in hectares, because hectares are easy to count. Connectivity disappears without anyone tallying it, and connectivity is what keeps a population functioning. It lets young animals find territory. It keeps gene pools mixing. It gives species somewhere to go when fire or heat makes a patch unliveable. Remove it and you do not get a smaller version of the same population. You get islands, each one quietly running down.

None of which is an argument against building houses. Sydney, Melbourne, Perth and South East Queensland all need them, and pretending otherwise loses the argument before it starts. The choice in front of us was never koalas or first home buyers. It is whether the corridor written into the plan gets bought and protected before the estate is drawn, and whether we cluster development around contiguous open space or spread it thin across the routes wildlife already uses. Same dwellings. Very different outcome. Four regions show why.

blocks.heading: One: the last chlamydia-free koala stronghold in the Sydney Basin
blocks.alt: A koala crossing a road at the edge of housing
blocks.caption: South-west Sydney holds something rare: the only koala population in the Sydney Basin still free of chlamydia, the disease that has hollowed out koala numbers across the eastern states.

flow.p: South-west Sydney holds something rare: the only koala population in the Sydney Basin still free of chlamydia, the disease that has hollowed out koala numbers across the eastern states. Surveys through 2021 and 2023 confirmed the Campbelltown koalas remain free of it. That is a genuine stronghold, and it is worth everything to protect.

The catch is that being disease-free is not the same as being safe. Research published in early 2025 by the University of Sydney found these koalas are highly inbred, with low genetic diversity, precisely because roads and cleared land have cut them off from populations further afield. A population that cannot mix cannot refresh its gene pool, and a population with a narrow gene pool is less able to adapt when a new threat, chlamydia included, arrives at its edge.

This is the quiet argument for connectivity, and it is more important than any single road crossing. Corridors are how genes move. They let young koalas disperse, find unrelated mates and keep the population resilient. Narrow the connections and you do not just make the koalas harder to see. You make them more fragile in ways that only show up a generation later. For a population like this one, the movement route is not a convenience. It is the difference between a stronghold that endures and one that slowly closes in on itself.

flow.h: 3,750 hectares: the reserve Melbourne is still assembling

flow.p: In 2010, in exchange for extending Melbourne’s urban growth boundary across the volcanic plains, the Victorian Government committed to a 15,000 hectare Western Grassland Reserve. Fifteen years on, roughly a quarter of that land has been secured. Call it 3,750 hectares of a 15,000 hectare commitment, with the rest still to come.

The lag is not a lack of will so much as a hard truth about this kind of conservation: buying land at scale is slow and expensive, and every year the acquisition takes, the land it is meant to protect keeps degrading under weeds and stock. Native temperate grassland is critically endangered, with around one per cent of its original extent remaining. The reserve is meant to hold what is left, along with the growling grass frog, the striped legless lizard, the spiny riceflower and the fat-tailed dunnart. This is exactly the kind of gap philanthropy and community effort exist to help close, alongside government, rather than wait on it.

The frogs show why the timing matters. Growling grass frogs survive as metapopulations strung along wetland chains, moving pond to pond across the Werribee, Merri and Darebin systems. Break the chain with a housing estate and the frogs upstream are not inconvenienced. They are alone.

flow.h: 12 kilometres a day: why Perth’s corridor problem is really a food problem

flow.p: That is roughly how far a male Carnaby’s black cockatoo will fly in a day to feed his mate while she sits on the nest. A useful reminder that a corridor is not only a path. It is a food supply, spread across a distance an animal can physically cover.

Carnaby’s breed in the Wheatbelt and spend most of the year feeding on Perth’s Swan Coastal Plain, in banksia woodland now reduced to around 40 per cent of its original extent and listed as endangered. The plain as a whole retains less than a third of its native vegetation. Every new estate on the northern sandplain removes another feeding stop and stretches the gap between the ones still standing. Volunteer counts have tracked steep declines in the birds using the plain.
In Perth, you can lose the corridor without clearing a single one of the remaining patches. You only have to remove enough of the stepping stones between them.

blocks.heading: 22 years: the crossing that has been working since 2004
blocks.alt: The planted wildlife overpass across Compton Road in Brisbane's south
blocks.caption: In 2004, Compton Road in Brisbane’s south was widened from two lanes to four.

flow.p: In 2004, Compton Road in Brisbane’s south was widened from two lanes to four. Rather than simply severing Karawatha Forest from the Kuraby bushlands, the upgrade included a vegetated land bridge over the road, underpasses beneath it, glider poles and a rope canopy bridge.

The overpass was planted out with local species, and by 2009 about 95 per cent of those plantings had survived. Monitoring by Griffith University and others has since recorded koalas, gliders, wallabies, echidnas, microbats, frogs and reptiles using it. It works because it was designed as a continuation of the forest rather than as an engineering afterthought, and it has been working for twenty-two years. Compton Road is proof that the science is settled and the outcome is achievable. The opportunity now is to make that standard the norm on every growth front, not the exception.

blocks.heading: The edge is not a choice
blocks.alt: Kangaroos grazing on a suburban backyard lawn
blocks.caption: Ask why a koala turns up in a backyard, or a wallaby on a school oval, and the honest answer is almost always that the interior it used to live in has gone, and the edge is what is left.

flow.p: Ask why a koala turns up in a backyard, or a wallaby on a school oval, and the honest answer is almost always that the interior it used to live in has gone, and the edge is what is left. Animals are not moving into our suburbs. Our suburbs moved onto their range, and the strip between the last house and the last tree is now the only cover, food and passage available.

Edges are hostile in ways a map never shows. Light, noise, weeds and traffic all push inward from the boundary, and so do our pets. Roaming pet cats reach densities of forty to seventy per square kilometre in Australian suburbs, killing thousands of native animals per square kilometre each year, and cats whose homes back onto bushland range into that bushland far more than cats living a few streets away.

blocks.alt: Native birds feeding in a suburban garden

flow.p: Australia also has its own edge specialist, and it is a native bird. The noisy miner thrives in remnants with a high ratio of edge to interior, where it aggressively drives out smaller woodland birds. Its behaviour is listed as a key threatening process under national environment law, and the Commonwealth’s own abatement advice is blunt about the fix: avoid increasing the ratio of edge to interior habitat.
A narrow corridor does precisely that. It is not a thin version of a forest. It is a long piece of edge.

flow.h: The corridor that makes things worse

flow.p: A corridor can be designed so poorly that it does more harm than good. Drawn too narrowly, squeezed in around everything else on a busy site, it can end up working against the animals it is meant to help. It looks like habitat. It reads as green on the plan. It draws animals in, and then it can deliver them to a four-lane road, a dog fence or a dead end. Ecologists have understood this for decades: a strip that funnels wildlife toward danger concentrates mortality rather than preventing it.
The encouraging part is that this is entirely avoidable at the design stage. It is why width and continuity are not bureaucratic detail. They are the difference between a corridor and a funnel.

blocks.heading: What separates a corridor from a green line on a plan
blocks.alt: Diagram comparing fragmented habitat patches with a wide, continuous corridor design
blocks.caption: Width, continuity, placement, permanence and buffers.

flow.p: Width. Narrow strips are all edge, and we have just seen what edge does. Width buys interior.
Continuity. A corridor with a break in it is a dead end, and a dead end is worse than nothing. It funnels animals into traffic and backyards.
Placement. Ridgelines, creek lines and wetland chains are where animals already move. Build across them and you sever the connection, no matter how much green space the plan contains in total.

Permanence. A corridor that can be rezoned is not yet secure. Land bought and reserved outperforms land still to be acquired, every single time. Melbourne’s grasslands show why locking in permanence early, and resourcing the acquisition to match, is worth the effort.

Buffers. Undeveloped land around high-value habitat lowers the edge to interior ratio and puts distance between wildlife and the things that kill it. Cluster the houses, keep the open space contiguous, and you get fewer collisions and fewer conflicts than the same number of dwellings spread thin across the same ground. It costs a developer very little, and it is one of the easiest wins to build into a plan from the start.

None of this is expensive next to the alternative. Retrofitting connectivity into a built-out suburb costs a fortune and rarely fully works. Protecting the route before the estate is drawn costs a fraction of it.

We have spent more than fifty years doing the patient version of this work, in partnership with governments, landholders and communities: buying the land that links the parks, funding the revegetation that closes the gaps, and backing the people restoring habitat on private property in the places the growth fronts are heading next.

The Bandicoot Superhighway in South Australia’s Mount Lofty Ranges is what that looks like on the ground. Delivered with the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, the Sturt Upper Reaches Landcare Group, the Nature Conservation Society of South Australia and the Australian Government, it reconnects fragmented habitat for the endangered southern brown bandicoot. In two years it restored connectivity across 216 hectares of priority habitat, put more than 34,000 native seedlings in the ground, and drew in over 900 people through planting days and workshops. Camera traps and citizen-science sightings have since confirmed the bandicoots are using the route to move, forage and survive. That is a corridor doing exactly what a corridor is for.
The science on connectivity is settled. What moves it from the plan to the ground is partnership, and the funding to buy and restore the ground before it is gone.

Which brings us back to the koala in south-west Sydney. Her stronghold will hold, or it will slowly close in around her. Either way, her daughters will need room to move and unrelated koalas to find, and the work in front of all of us is making sure the connections are still there for them.

title: Your Backyard Is Habitat Too: Help Native Wildlife
standfirst: A quarter-acre block, a shared courtyard, three pots on a balcony rail. To a sugar glider hunting for somewhere safe to land, any of them might be the difference between making the crossing and turning back. Here is how a small patch of Australian natives starts pulling its weight.
hero_alt: A green and brown bird with a pale bill and a blue eye, perched on a garden fence with palm fronds behind it.
description: Most of the green on a city map is mown lawn and imported hedge, which native animals cannot use. A backyard, a courtyard or a balcony planted with local natives becomes the next safe step for bees, lizards, microbats and birds.

flow.p: A quarter-acre block, a shared courtyard, three pots on a balcony rail. To a sugar glider hunting for somewhere safe to land, any of them might be the difference between making the crossing and turning back. Here is how a small patch of Australian natives starts pulling its weight.

blocks.heading: The map is emptier than it looks
blocks.alt: An aerial view of suburban rooftops and a curving street, with almost no tree canopy between the houses.
blocks.caption: Zoom in on any Australian city and the green bits look generous: parks, ovals, the odd remnant of bush.

flow.p: Zoom in on any Australian city and the green bits look generous: parks, ovals, the odd remnant of bush. Look closer and most of it is mown grass and imported hedges, which to a native animal is about as useful as a car park. Real bushland has been cut into islands, and a lot of our wildlife simply can’t get between them. A pardalote won’t cross a wide stretch of open lawn. A native bee rarely forages more than a few hundred metres from where it nested.

This is where you come in, and it is less grand than it sounds. You plant one flowering grevillea. Someone two streets over plants a bottlebrush. A council street tree sits in between. Suddenly there is a chain of feeding and resting spots, a set of stepping stones an animal can hop along without ever breaking cover. Ecologists have measured this: gardens full of local native plants carry more insects, more birds and more small mammals than the tidiest exotic yard on the block. Your backyard doesn’t have to be a national park. It only has to be the next safe step.

flow.h: Who turns up when you plant the right thing

flow.p: The guest list is stranger and more charming than you’d expect.

blocks.alt: A blue-banded bee gripping a purple flower.

flow.p: Take the blue-banded bee, a fuzzy native with iridescent stripes and a genuine party trick. Some flowers lock their pollen away and release it only to a very particular vibration. The blue-banded bee clamps on and shivers its flight muscles at around 350 beats a second, a technique called buzz pollination, and the pollen comes loose in a puff. Introduced honeybees can’t do it at all. Your tomatoes, as it happens, adore a blue-banded bee.

Australia has close to 2,000 native bee species, and most are solitary, stingless, or both. In warmer regions you might host a hive of sugarbag bees, tiny black stingless natives that store honey in little wax pots and defend the nest by gluing intruders in place with resin.

blocks.alt: A blue-tongue lizard resting in leaf litter beneath flowering wattle.

flow.p: Then there is the blue-tongue lizard, the slow, sun-loving reptile that treats a garden like an all-you-can-eat buffet for snails and slugs. Keep a few blue-tongues happy and you barely need snail bait. You certainly shouldn’t use it either, because the poison travels straight up the food chain and into them.
After dark, a single insect-eating microbat can put away close to half its body weight in mosquitoes and moths in one night. Plant for the insects and the bats feed themselves.

blocks.alt: A honeyeater feeding among red and orange kangaroo paw flowers.

flow.p: And for sheer romance, watch a honeyeater work a kangaroo paw. The flower dabs pollen onto the precise spot on the bird’s forehead that will brush the next bloom, turning the bird into an unpaid courier. Superb fairy-wrens go one better in the courtship stakes: the males pluck bright yellow petals and present them to the females, which is either deeply sweet or wildly try-hard, depending on your mood.

flow.h: Wild is doing more work than tidy

flow.p: Here is the good news for anyone who resents weekend garden chores. A slightly messy patch is better habitat than a manicured one.

Leave the leaf litter under your shrubs and you give skinks, spiders and beetles somewhere to shelter and breed, which feeds everything above them. Plant in layers, groundcover beneath shrubs beneath a small tree, and you hand different animals different rooms in the same house. Set out a shallow dish of water with a rock in the middle and keep it topped up through summer, and you have built a lifeline for the cost of nothing. Skip the pesticides completely; a garden full of predators sorts out its own pests inside a season or two.

blocks.alt: A bird perched on a timber balcony railing, with garden foliage behind it.

flow.p: No garden at all? A balcony still counts. One pot of correa flowers right through the cold months when almost nothing else does, feeding birds in the lean season. Native violet spreads happily in shade. A kangaroo paw or a compact grevillea in a decent pot will pull nectar-feeders in several storeys up. Bees and birds find balconies far more often than you would guess, and a rail full of natives becomes another stepping stone above the street.

blocks.heading: The secret ingredient is local
blocks.alt: Rows of seedlings and shrubs growing on at a community nursery, with people working among them.
blocks.caption: One catch: not all natives are equal.

flow.p: One catch: not all natives are equal. A plant bred for a nursery three states away might flower at the wrong time for your local pollinators, or feed nothing much at all. What our wildlife evolved alongside are local-provenance plants, grown from seed collected nearby and matched to the exact birds and insects already living in your postcode.

The people who understand this best are community-led native plant nurseries. These are small, often volunteer-run outfits that collect local seed, propagate the right species for their patch, and put affordable, genuinely useful plants into the hands of the people around them. They are rebuilding habitat one tubestock tray at a time, and they are almost always short of hands.

We back this work through our community of native plant nurseries, because a nursery growing local species is a habitat factory for an entire suburb. Visit one, ask what belongs where you live, and take home a plant or two. Better still, offer them a Saturday morning.

You don’t need to rewild an acre. Put in a single flowering native this weekend, let the leaf litter lie where it falls, and set out a dish of water. Something small and winged and entirely Australian will find it. Multiply that by a street, then a suburb, then a city, and the map starts filling back in.

title: A million reasons to say thank you
standfirst: The last few years have been significant ones for FNPW. A national strategy that is already delivering. A tree planting program that has passed one million trees in the ground. Partnerships that are deeper, more ambitious, and built for the long term. None of it happened by accident, and none of it happened alone.
hero_alt: Supporters gathered at Lane Cove National Park to mark one million trees planted
description: One million trees in the ground, a strategy that is delivering, and partnerships built for the long term. David Knowles reflects on eight years with the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, three of them as President & Chair.

flow.p: The last few years have been significant ones for FNPW. A national strategy that is already delivering. A tree planting program that has passed one million trees in the ground. Partnerships that are deeper, more ambitious, and built for the long term. None of it happened by accident, and none of it happened alone.

David Knowles has been part of this organisation for eight years, three of them as President & Chair, and as he steps back from that role, we wanted to take a moment to reflect on what we have built together.
If there’s a thread that runs through everything FNPW achieved during David’s time on the board, it’s the shift toward thinking at a national scale.

“The organisation has taken a leap forward in its approach to tackling the problems we are here to solve,” David reflects. “Taking a national view and focusing on the most important areas, where we can have the greatest impact, across Australia, is absolutely the right thing to do.”

That thinking took its clearest form in FNPW 2025-2028 strategic plan, Partnering for Impact, which David helped shape alongside the board and executive team. “Being part of developing that strategy was really enjoyable,” he says, “and we are already starting to see its impact. Its impact should be felt well beyond 2028.”

blocks.heading: One trowel, one million reasons
blocks.alt: A tree seedling going into the ground at a community planting day
blocks.caption: Ask David to name a moment that has stayed with him, and he goes straight to Lane Cove National Park, and the day our tree planting program hit one million trees.

flow.p: Ask David to name a moment that has stayed with him, and he goes straight to Lane Cove National Park, and the day our tree planting program hit one million trees.
“It was a standout moment because it involved marking a milestone as well as actually planting a living tree into the Earth,” he says. “I still have the trowel and I intend to keep it.”
That detail says a lot. One million is a number that matters. A trowel pressed into soil is the feeling behind it.

flow.h: Growing with the urgency of the moment

flow.p: Conservation has become a more urgent, more scrutinised space over the past eight years, and FNPW has grown with it.

“As well as the environment itself, we have evolved our thinking in terms of who we partner with and who funds our work,” David says. “Those funders and partners have all become more sophisticated over the last few years, and I expect they will continue on that path.”

What held steady through all of that change was a clear sense of purpose. “With any charity, it is always about the mission and vision,” he reflects. “You can never lose sight of the reason you exist.”

When we asked David what he believes sets FNPW apart, his answer was simple. “FNPW has the ability to bring everything together. We can bring important initiatives to life and we can often turn good ideas into bigger and better ideas that result in more impact.”

That capacity to convene, connect, and amplify is something we see reflected in every partnership we hold, from Traditional Custodians and scientists to corporate supporters and on-the-ground conservation teams.

blocks.heading: To everyone who made it possible
blocks.alt: David Knowles passing the microphone at an FNPW event
blocks.caption: David also had something he wanted to say to the donors and supporters who have backed this work.

flow.p: David also had something he wanted to say to the donors and supporters who have backed this work.

“The first thing I would do is thank them for their support, and their care for the environment and our amazing wildlife. I would say that they support a great organisation doing important work well. Their support will be critical going forward as we look to continue our increasingly urgent work.”
We couldn’t put it better ourselves.
Beyond the milestones, what David says he’s most proud of is the people. “When I look around the boardroom table, I think we have a group of really high-calibre, experienced and committed people.”

A strong strategy and the right people to carry it forward. At our most recent AGM, David passed the role of President & Chair to Kelly O’Shanassy, and left behind an organisation well placed to meet what comes next. That’s not a bad thing to leave behind at all.
“I care about the things that drew me to FNPW in the first place, so I’ll stay involved. At the same time, I’ll create a bit more space in my life.”
David, from everyone at FNPW, our partners, our supporters, and every species this work exists to protect: thank you. It has been a privilege to do this alongside you.

related.title: From advocate to chair: nature, ambition, and what comes next
related.blurb: Kelly O'Shanassy, who led the Australian Conservation Foundation for nearly 12 years, has taken up the role of President and Chair of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife. She talks about business, climate, and what she wants FNPW to become.

title: From advocate to chair: nature, ambition, and what comes next
standfirst: After nearly 12 years as CEO of the Australian Conservation Foundation, Kelly O’Shanassy is stepping into a new role as President and Chair of FNPW. We sat down with her to find out what drew her here, and what she’s got planned.
hero_alt: Kelly O'Shanassy outdoors, smiling to camera.
description: Kelly O'Shanassy, who led the Australian Conservation Foundation for nearly 12 years, has taken up the role of President and Chair of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife. She talks about business, climate, and what she wants FNPW to become.

flow.p: After nearly 12 years as CEO of the Australian Conservation Foundation, Kelly O’Shanassy is stepping into a new role as President and Chair of FNPW. We sat down with her to find out what drew her here, and what she’s got planned.

There’s a certain kind of person who walks into a room, whether that’s a boardroom, a parliamentary briefing, or even the mining lobby, and doesn’t adjust their message to suit the audience. They bring the audience to them.
Kelly O’Shanassy is that kind of person.

For those who follow the conservation sector, the appointment makes complete sense. For those meeting Kelly for the first time, it might just change how you think about what leadership in this space can look like.
Leaving a job you love is never simple. Leaving one you’ve held for over a decade, where you watched a team achieve things people told you were impossible, is something else entirely.
“It was 11 years and we had kept innovating and changing things up because we needed to,” Kelly says. “In the end, I thought I’ve done everything I wanted to do.”

That decision led her toward boards, a way, she says, to have significant leadership impact across multiple organisations rather than within one. But when FNPW came into the picture, something specific caught her attention: the tangibility of the work.

“I wanted to experience working in an organisation that had very tangible impact,” she says. “Like you can go and touch the things that the foundation does.” After more than a decade of advocacy, pushing governments, shifting policy, trying to trace which strategy finally broke through, the idea of standing in a forest that is genuinely, physically protected felt like a different kind of reward entirely.

There is something about FNPW’s character that resonated with Kelly on a more personal level too. “The positive, joyful, solutions-focused nature of the foundation resonates very strongly with me,” she says. Throughout her career, Kelly has maintained that people should work in organisations where the goals align with their own values. FNPW’s clarity of purpose, protecting wildlife, growing national parks, healing land, was a big part of what drew her here.

So was the science. Kelly is a scientist by training, and she doesn’t soften the data. “Habitat destruction is the major driver of extinction in Australia. The last remaining habitats are absolutely critical to protect.” She also makes the connection between nature and people with a directness that cuts through the abstraction. “People love nature in Australia,” she says. “They don’t understand it’s in trouble.” That gap, between love and understanding, is where she sees the greatest opportunity.

flow.h: “I miss the opportunity to shape hearts and minds. But I’m going to have that in this role now. And I’m very excited.”

blocks.alt: Kelly O'Shanassy in conversation, seated and gesturing as she speaks.

flow.p: If there’s one thing Kelly has learned from years of working across NGOs, government, unions, and corporations, it’s that the boardroom is one of the most powerful rooms in the building, and that conservation has every right to be in it.

The shift, she says, is already underway. Climate hit boardrooms first, and even then it took the better part of a decade to be taken seriously. Nature is following the same trajectory, and faster. People don’t always see how it impacts their company, she observes, but with the global biodiversity framework now in place and nature risk disclosures moving toward mandatory status, that’s changing quickly. Businesses are being required to understand both their dependencies on nature and their impact on it, essentially producing a profit and loss statement for the natural world. The same rigour companies apply to their financial position is now being applied to their relationship with ecosystems.

Kelly is clear-eyed about why that matters. Corporations, she points out, are not people. They don’t have hearts and they don’t act out of goodness alone. Something can happen in workplaces, she observes, where the humanness of the people inside gets stripped away by the institution around them. But it is still humans making the decisions, and those humans are responsible to a wide circle of stakeholders: staff, customers, investors, shareholders, and the communities their business depends on. Nature risk disclosures make the stakes legible in the language boards actually respond to.

Her view on corporate partnerships is direct and grounded in what businesses actually respond to. “If you do this, you will benefit. And if you don’t, you are going to be exposed to pretty big risks.” She’s also quick to point out that sustainability can’t be reduced to double-sided printing and LED light bulbs. The business model itself has to drive the change. For companies that are heavily exposed to natural resources, that shift is not optional, and Kelly sees organisations like FNPW as essential partners in helping them get there. Whether that’s through corporate volunteering, land protection partnerships, or deeper strategic alignment, the through-line is always the same: this is good for your business, and it is also genuinely good for the world.

She’s also worried about something subtler than greenwashing: green hushing, where organisations become so afraid of scrutiny that they stop making environmental commitments at all. Her answer to that is characteristically practical. If a company is 70% of the way toward its environmental goals, staying quiet about it helps no one. “Seventy percent is all right,” she says. “We’ll get the next 30 and then we’ll get the next lot after that.” Progress matters more than perfection, and silence is not a strategy.

flow.h: Climate, nature, and the power of unusual alliances

flow.p: Kelly has been deeply embedded in national net zero planning, and she’s impatient with the idea that climate and nature are running on separate tracks. “Protecting land protects habitat. Protecting habitat protects species.” The reverse is equally true: when nature collapses, so do the systems humans rely on for food, water, clean air, and the landscapes we want our children to inherit.

She’s pointed about what’s at stake in the near term. “Kids aren’t going to be able to see koalas in the wild in New South Wales,” she says plainly. “They won’t. It’s very clear unless we change.” Her view is that the story of nature’s crisis needs to be told in exactly those terms, connected to now, connected to people, and always paired with a solution. “We have to link it to how it’s impacting people now,” she says. “It’s not a future problem.”

Getting that message through, she has found, works best when it comes from unexpected corners. One of the things Kelly is most proud of from her time at ACF is what happened when the environment movement and the business community stopped fighting each other over nature protection laws and started looking for common ground instead. “As much alignment as you can get as possible across unusual partners has always had the greatest impact,” she says.

After years of opposition, the two sides identified the 70% they agreed on and took that to government together, leaving the remaining 30% for ministers to navigate. The result was a reform that had stalled for nearly a decade. “There’s nothing like when an environmentalist and a business person agrees and goes in and talks to Parliament on that,” she says. It’s a model she brings with her to FNPW, rooted in the belief that big-picture ambition from the environment movement, combined with the know-how and resources of business, can genuinely accelerate change.

flow.h: What does the best version of FNPW look like?

flow.p: Kelly’s leadership philosophy is grounded in people, not titles. “Great organisations are about the collective of humans inside it, not just about the leader, not about the chair.” She talks about wanting every person connected to FNPW, staff, board, councillors, donors, volunteers, to see the positive impact they’re creating and to feel genuinely equipped to drive more of it.

Focus, she says, matters more than most people realise. “If you’re doing too many things, you’re not going to do any of those things very well.” The foundation has clear goals. Her job is to help everyone inside and around it feel themselves in those goals, and to have the systems in place that let people really shine.

Outside of the work, Kelly kayaks, hikes, and plays the ukulele. “It’s a joyful little instrument,” she says. “You can’t take it too seriously.” She tells a story about the very beginning of her time at ACF, when she got so busy she went three months without kayaking. Walking to a workshop one morning, she crossed the Yarra River and felt the absence of it like something physical. “The love I had for that river.” After that, she protected the time.

Nature, in her experience, is not a backdrop to the work. It’s what motivates it. “Love and fury are both important,” she says. “But ultimately, everyone wants to have a happy life. Everyone wants to see a positive future. You need to have that joyful element.”

flow.h: A message to the FNPW community

flow.p: For those meeting Kelly for the first time through this article, her message is both grounding and galvanising.

“What FNPW does, what we do together, is incredibly important to protect nature in Australia. It makes a difference, a big difference. You can feel and touch the places that it’s made a difference to.” And she’s not asking people to slow down and appreciate that. She’s asking them to use it as fuel. “We need to keep going and go as fast as we can because this works, but needs to work harder to achieve the goals that we need to achieve and protect those species that are at risk of extinction.”

For the moments when the scale of the challenge starts to feel too big, she offers a reframe rather than reassurance. Kelly invokes Nelson Mandela: things only seem impossible until they’re done. It’s not a platitude in her hands. It’s a pattern she has watched repeat across her career, in policy wins people said would never happen, in renewable energy targets that once seemed absurd, in rivers that ran dry and then ran again.
Her advice to anyone who needs it is the same advice she lives by: look back to dream forward.

Look back at when almost no land in Australia was protected. When renewable energy was a fringe idea. When the Murray-Darling ran so low you couldn’t move sediment through its mouth. Now look at where we stand. Twenty-two percent of land protected. Nearly half of Australia’s electricity coming from renewables at peak times. More than 3,200 billion litres of water flowing down the Murray again. “And then dream forward about where we’re going to be next,” she says.

The progress has not been fast or easy. But Kelly’s point is that the future doesn’t move in a straight line. “It continuously accelerates if we put the right effort in.” She was there for the hard early years. She watched the impossible become possible, more than once. And she is here, now, because she believes we can continue to increase that momentum.
Kelly O’Shanassy has officially taken up the role of President and Chair of FNPW at the latest AGM. We are so glad to have her.

title: Bringing Back the Growling Grass Frog
standfirst: There is something quietly extraordinary about a frog call echoing across a restored wetland at dusk. For people who know what that sound means, and what it took to get there, it carries real weight.
hero_alt: A Growling Grass Frog at the edge of a wetland.
description: The Growling Grass Frog is listed as Vulnerable and has vanished from much of its former range. At Winton Wetlands in north-east Victoria, a founding population of 60 to 65 frogs is now in place, with monitoring running to March 2026 to see whether they breed.

flow.p: There is something quietly extraordinary about a frog call echoing across a restored wetland at dusk. For people who know what that sound means, and what it took to get there, it carries real weight.

The Growling Grass Frog (Litoria raniformis) was once a familiar presence across the wetlands and waterways of south-eastern Australia. Today it is nationally listed as Vulnerable under the EPBC Act, its numbers diminished by habitat loss, altered water regimes, disease and declining water quality. In many parts of its former range, it has simply disappeared.
That is why what is happening at Winton Wetlands in north-east Victoria matters so much.

blocks.heading: Meet the Growling Grass Frog
blocks.alt: A Growling Grass Frog, bright green with dark blotches.
blocks.caption: Despite its name, the Growling Grass Frog is actually one of Australia’s more striking amphibians.

flow.p: Despite its name, the Growling Grass Frog is actually one of Australia’s more striking amphibians. It is large by local standards, reaching up to 10 centimetres, and is easily recognised by its bright green back marked with dark blotches, a pale belly and a distinctive dark stripe running through the eye. Its call is a low, rasping growl, which is where the name comes from, and during breeding season it can be heard carrying across open water on warm evenings.

It is also, ecologically speaking, a species that punches well above its weight. The Growling Grass Frog is considered an indicator species, meaning its presence, and its breeding success, reflect the broader health of the wetland system around it. When this frog thrives, it tells you that water quality is good, vegetation is functioning, and the hydrological cycles that underpin wetland life are working as they should. When it disappears, something significant has shifted.

blocks.heading: Why Winton Wetlands
blocks.alt: Open water at Winton Wetlands in north-east Victoria.
blocks.caption: Located between Benalla and Glenrowan in north-east Victoria, Winton Wetlands has a story worth knowing.

flow.p: Located between Benalla and Glenrowan in north-east Victoria, Winton Wetlands has a story worth knowing. The site was once a water storage reservoir, decommissioned and left degraded for years. Over time, sustained investment and genuine commitment to ecological restoration has transformed it into a functioning natural swamp and wetland, receiving environmental water flows and supporting ongoing woodland recovery across the surrounding landscape.

It is exactly the kind of place where careful, science-led conservation can make a lasting difference. The wetland now supports a purpose-built amphibian breeding and quarantine facility, a dedicated interpretation centre for visitors, and an active restoration program. The groundwork has been laid thoughtfully and well.

blocks.alt: Shallow water and wetland vegetation at the restored site.

flow.p: Historically, the Growling Grass Frog was present in this region. The goal now is to bring it back.

blocks.heading: How the translocation works
blocks.alt: The translocation site at Winton Wetlands.
blocks.caption: The translocation began in late 2025 with frogs collected near Bendigo.

flow.p: With support from FNPW, delivery partner Swamps, Rivers and Ranges, the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA), and the Wettenhall Foundation, a carefully managed translocation program got underway in late 2025.

A cohort of 35 to 40 adult frogs was collected from an established population near Bendigo in central Victoria. After a 30-day quarantine and health screening at the Winton facility, they were released on site alongside the 25 frogs already living there, creating a founding population of 60 to 65 animals.

blocks.alt: Habitat where the founding population was released.

flow.p: From there, monitoring continues through to March 2026, tracking survival, movement, habitat use and most importantly, whether the frogs are breeding. Breeding success is the real measure. It signals not just that the frogs have survived the move, but that the wetland is genuinely capable of supporting the full life cycle of a sensitive amphibian species. That is a meaningful ecological threshold.

blocks.heading: More than one species
blocks.alt: The wider wetland system at Winton Wetlands.
blocks.caption: A restored wetland that can support a Growling Grass Frog population is a wetland that supports a lot of other life too.

flow.p: A restored wetland that can support a Growling Grass Frog population is a wetland that supports a lot of other life too. Waterbirds, invertebrates, native fish and riparian plants all benefit from the same conditions the frog needs. Investing in the recovery of an indicator species is, in a real sense, investing in the recovery of an entire ecosystem.

It is also about building knowledge. Every translocation generates practical data on quarantine protocols, release methods and monitoring approaches that will inform future recovery efforts across north-east Victoria and southern New South Wales, where the species has declined significantly.

blocks.heading: A Future worth protecting
blocks.alt: A Growling Grass Frog at the water's edge.
blocks.caption: The Growling Grass Frog will not recover overnight.

flow.p: The Growling Grass Frog will not recover overnight. But with the right conditions, the right partners, and sustained care for the landscape it depends on, recovery is genuinely possible.

That is what this project is about. Not just returning a species to a wetland, but demonstrating that large-scale ecological restoration, done well and done with patience, can rebuild the complexity that threatened wildlife needs to survive.
When that growl echoes across Winton Wetlands again on a warm spring evening, it will mean something.
FNPW contributed $36,000 to support the translocation and monitoring program at Winton Wetlands, delivered in partnership with Swamps, Rivers and Ranges and DEECA.

related.title: The Land Behind Australia's World Heritage Bid
related.blurb: A 4,500-hectare acquisition adds Balcoracana Paddock to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, protecting Adnyamathanha Country, yellow-footed rock wallabies and the fossil beds behind Australia's Flinders Ranges World Heritage nomination.

title: The Land Behind Australia's World Heritage Bid
standfirst: How a 4,500-hectare acquisition in the Flinders Ranges is protecting ancient Country, rare wildlife, and half a billion years of Earth history
hero_alt: Rocky ridges and creek country in the northern Flinders Ranges.
description: A 4,500-hectare acquisition adds Balcoracana Paddock to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, protecting Adnyamathanha Country, yellow-footed rock wallabies and the fossil beds behind Australia's Flinders Ranges World Heritage nomination.

flow.p: Deep in the northern Flinders Ranges, about 17 kilometres east of the small settlement of Blinman, sits a stretch of country that has been holding its breath for a very long time.

Balcoracana Paddock is part of the Bunkers Range on Adnyamathanha Country. Its gorges and creek beds hold permanent water. Its cave systems shelter yellow-footed rock wallabies. And beneath its surface lies some of the most scientifically significant fossil records on Earth: sedimentary sequences from the Cambrian period documenting more than 500 million years of life.
This land has now been permanently added to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park.

We partnered with the Australian Government and the SA Department for Environment and Water to acquire Balcoracana Paddock, adding approximately 4,500 hectares of conservation-significant country to the park’s protected estate. The acquisition was also supported through the Federal Government’s Protecting Important Biodiversity Areas Program.

blocks.heading: A nomination a decade in the making
blocks.alt: Gorge and creek country in the Bunkers Range.
blocks.caption: Seven properties underpin the Flinders Ranges World Heritage bid.

flow.p: The timing is significant. In February 2026, Australia formally submitted the Flinders Ranges World Heritage nomination to UNESCO’s World Heritage Centre in Paris, and the nomination has since been accepted for assessment. A final decision from the World Heritage Committee is expected in mid-2027. It is a milestone a decade in the making, backed by a 368-page submission and nearly 4,000 pages of supporting documentation.

Balcoracana Paddock is one of seven properties whose geological record underpins that bid. The Flinders Ranges is the only place on Earth where the continuous formation of the earliest complex animal life, between 672 and 510 million years ago, can be observed across three geological periods: the Cryogenian, Ediacaran, and Cambrian.

For the Adnyamathanha people, whose connection to this Country runs far deeper than any pastoral boundary, the nomination and the acquisition carry real meaning together. UNESCO requires World Heritage bids to be supported and consented to by all relevant First Nations communities. Last year, the Adnyamathanha Common Law Holders provided that consent.

As an addition to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, Balcoracana Paddock now falls under the existing co-management agreement between Adnyamathanha native title holders and the South Australian Government, expanding Traditional Owners’ formal decision-making role across the landscape.

Adnyamathanha Senior Elder Charles Jackson OAM has spoken of the importance of Adnyamathanha people coming together on this nomination, and of their cultural information placing them front and centre on the world stage. The land acquisition is part of that same commitment.

blocks.heading: Somewhere to go
blocks.alt: Nankeen kestrels in the ranges above the paddock.
blocks.caption: For wildlife, the benefits are immediate.

flow.p: For wildlife, the benefits are immediate. Removing stock grazing allows native vegetation to recover across the creek beds and drainage areas where threatened plant species are already returning.

The land connects directly into the Bounceback Program’s existing predator and grazing management regime, which has driven significant recovery of yellow-footed rock wallabies, short-tailed grasswrens, and echidnas across the broader Ikara-Flinders landscape. Western quolls, successfully reintroduced to the park, have been recorded moving northeast toward Balcoracana Paddock.
This acquisition gives them somewhere to go.

The Flinders Ranges was recently named the only Australian destination on Lonely Planet’s must-visit list for 2026. World Heritage listing, if confirmed, would cement that recognition on a global scale. But the case for protecting this country doesn’t rest on tourism or titles. It rests on what’s here: ancient fossils, rare animals, living culture, and a landscape that holds an irreplaceable record of life on Earth.

blocks.heading: Growing national parks
blocks.alt: A graphic marking the Balcoracana Paddock acquisition.
blocks.caption: Growing national parks is one of our three core commitments.

flow.p: Growing national parks is one of our three core commitments. Balcoracana Paddock is exactly the kind of acquisition that makes it real.

related.title: Growing Resilience from the Ground Up
related.blurb: Restoration begins with seed, and Australia is short of it. Through the Landscape Resilience Program, the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife is backing Trees For Life to collect local provenance seed and grow the native plants that damaged landscapes need.

title: Why Expanding National Parks Matters for Australia’s Future
standfirst: From the air, Australia’s landscapes look vast and uninterrupted. But on the ground, many ecosystems are now broken into smaller and smaller pieces.
hero_alt: Bushland stretching to the horizon inside an Australian national park.
description: Australia's ecosystems are broken into smaller and smaller pieces, and wildlife pays the price. Adding land to the national park estate reconnects those fragments, protects whole systems and gives threatened species room to recover.

flow.p: From the air, Australia’s landscapes look vast and uninterrupted. But on the ground, many ecosystems are now broken into smaller and smaller pieces.

A woodland might survive on one side of a road, while cleared paddocks stretch out on the other. A wetland may still fill with water after rain, but the surrounding habitat that once supported birds, fish and amphibians has disappeared. A forest may remain standing, but the animals that once moved freely through it now encounter fences, farmland or towns.
For wildlife, these invisible boundaries matter.

Animals that once travelled kilometres across a landscape in search of food, water or breeding partners now find themselves confined to isolated pockets of habitat. Over time, those pockets shrink, species disappear and ecological systems begin to unravel.
Expanding national parks is one of the few tools we have to reverse that process.

When land is added to the national park estate, those fragments begin to reconnect. Landscapes become larger and more continuous again. Rivers flow through protected catchments. Forests link to woodlands. Wetlands reconnect with floodplains.
Instead of protecting nature in small islands, we begin protecting whole systems.

National parks are not simply scenic places set aside for recreation. They are landscapes where ecological processes are allowed to continue largely uninterrupted. Fire cycles, animal migrations, pollination, seed dispersal and soil regeneration all play out across space and time.
And when these processes are protected, nature has the chance to recover.

blocks.heading: What a National Park Actually Is
blocks.alt: A national park sign at the edge of protected bushland.
blocks.caption: Across Australia, national parks are areas of land legally reserved for conservation.

flow.p: Across Australia, national parks are areas of land legally reserved for conservation. They are established under state and federal legislation and managed to protect biodiversity, ecosystems and cultural heritage.
Unlike most other land uses, conservation becomes the primary purpose of the landscape. Development pressures are reduced, and long-term management plans guide how the park is protected and restored.

Australia’s first national park, Royal National Park south of Sydney, was created in 1879, making it one of the earliest national parks in the world. Over time, the system expanded to include alpine regions, rainforests, arid landscapes and marine ecosystems.

Today, national parks form part of Australia’s protected area network, which conservation scientists consider the most effective tool for ensuring threatened species and ecosystems can survive and recover.

flow.h: What Changes When Land Becomes a National Park

flow.p: When land is added to a national park, its future changes dramatically.

Instead of being managed for agriculture, development or extraction, the focus shifts to ecological protection and long-term restoration. Park managers develop detailed management plans to identify the landscape’s key ecological values and the threats that need to be addressed.
These plans guide everything from fire management and weed control to wildlife monitoring and habitat restoration.

In many cases, newly protected landscapes require significant ecological repair. Areas that were previously cleared or heavily grazed often need revegetation and soil stabilisation before native ecosystems can return.
Over time, natural regeneration begins. Native plants recolonise the landscape, soil health improves, and habitats become suitable again for wildlife.

blocks.heading: Bringing Wildlife Back
blocks.alt: A native marsupial moving through low understorey.
blocks.caption: One of the most important roles national parks play is supporting the recovery of threatened species.

flow.p: One of the most important roles national parks play is supporting the recovery of threatened species.
Australia has lost more mammals than any other continent since European settlement. Many species declined after habitat clearing and the arrival of introduced predators such as foxes and feral cats.
Protected landscapes allow conservation programs to reverse some of these losses.

In South Australia’s Flinders Ranges, the long-running Bounceback program removed feral goats, foxes and rabbits from national parks to allow native ecosystems to recover. The work has helped restore habitat and made it possible to reintroduce locally extinct species.
In recent years, species such as western quolls and brushtail possums have been successfully reintroduced to protected areas in the region and are now breeding in the wild again.
These kinds of projects show what becomes possible when landscapes are protected and actively managed.
National parks also support wildlife corridors that allow animals to move between habitats. This connectivity is increasingly important as species shift their ranges in response to climate change.

blocks.heading: Protecting Entire Ecosystems
blocks.alt: Layers of native vegetation in a healthy woodland.
blocks.caption: Conservation is not only about individual species.

flow.p: Conservation is not only about individual species. It is about protecting the ecological systems that sustain life.

Healthy ecosystems are built on complex interactions between plants, animals, insects, fungi and microorganisms. Pollinators support flowering plants. Fungi recycle nutrients. Vegetation stabilises soils and protects waterways.
National parks protect these relationships by safeguarding large areas where natural processes can continue.
These landscapes also provide important environmental services that people rely on. Intact ecosystems help filter water, store carbon, reduce erosion and buffer the impacts of extreme weather.
In a warming climate, protected areas can also act as climate refuges, providing cooler, more stable habitats where species can persist as surrounding landscapes change.

blocks.heading: Protecting Culture and Country
blocks.alt: A rocky outcrop in a protected landscape of cultural significance.
blocks.caption: Many national parks are also places of deep cultural significance.

flow.p: Many national parks are also places of deep cultural significance.
Across Australia, protected landscapes contain Aboriginal cultural sites, rock art, ceremonial grounds and places tied to thousands of years of cultural knowledge.

Increasingly, national parks are being co-managed with Traditional Owners. These partnerships recognise the role First Nations peoples have played in caring for Country for tens of thousands of years and ensure that cultural knowledge continues to guide land management.
Traditional fire practices, seasonal knowledge and cultural stewardship are increasingly recognised as critical parts of modern conservation.
Land outside protected areas can change quickly.

It can be cleared, developed or fragmented as economic pressures shift. National park designation provides a stronger level of long-term protection and ensures landscapes are managed primarily for ecological health.
Expanding protected areas also improves connectivity across landscapes. Larger, linked ecosystems allow wildlife populations to move, adapt and maintain genetic diversity.
For conservation scientists, scale matters.
Small, isolated reserves can protect individual sites, but large connected landscapes are far more effective at sustaining biodiversity over the long term.

blocks.heading: Creating Space for Nature to Recover
blocks.alt: Regenerating bushland on land added to a national park.
blocks.caption: At FNPW, expanding protected areas is a key part of how we help nature recover.

flow.p: At FNPW, expanding protected areas is a key part of how we help nature recover.

By acquiring and protecting land adjacent to existing national parks, we can strengthen entire landscapes rather than protecting isolated pockets of habitat. These additions expand wildlife corridors, protect critical ecosystems and allow restoration work to occur at scale.
Healthy ecosystems take time to recover. But when land is protected, given space to regenerate and managed carefully, nature has a remarkable ability to bounce back.
Expanding national parks is ultimately about giving that recovery a chance.
Because protecting landscapes today helps ensure Australia’s wildlife, ecosystems and natural heritage continue to thrive long into the future.

title: Growing Resilience from the Ground Up
standfirst: Restoring native vegetation is one of the most practical and powerful ways we can help heal land, rebuild biodiversity, and create healthier habitats for wildlife and communities.
hero_alt: Rows of native tubestock seedlings ready for planting at a nursery.
description: Restoration begins with seed, and Australia is short of it. Through the Landscape Resilience Program, the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife is backing Trees For Life to collect local provenance seed and grow the native plants that damaged landscapes need.

flow.p: Restoring native vegetation is one of the most practical and powerful ways we can help heal land, rebuild biodiversity, and create healthier habitats for wildlife and communities.
But successful restoration begins long before the first tree is planted.
It begins with seed.
This is where Trees For Life plays such an important role. Based in South Australia, they help grow the native seed and plants that restoration projects across the country depend on.
Together, through our Landscape Resilience Program, we’re supporting seed collection and nursery efforts that make recovery possible.

blocks.heading: Why seeds matter in restoration
blocks.alt: Native seed held in a hand after collection.
blocks.caption: Every healthy ecosystem starts with the right plants in the right place.

flow.p: Every healthy ecosystem starts with the right plants in the right place.
When we restore degraded bushland, reconnect fragmented habitats, or revegetate land after fire or flood, we rely on native seedstock to bring these landscapes back to life.
Seed is not simply a supply issue. It is a biodiversity issue.

In ecological restoration, it is essential that plants come from the local region and are adapted to local soils, rainfall patterns, temperatures, and relationships with wildlife. This is known as local provenance, and it plays a critical role in long-term survival and ecosystem health.
Without enough locally appropriate seed, restoration efforts slow down, projects are delayed, and biodiversity outcomes are compromised.
Australia is currently facing a growing shortage of native seed, particularly for region-specific and hard-to-grow species that are vital for healthy bushland recovery.
FNPW’s Landscape Resilience Program was created in response to this challenge, helping increase the supply of native, local provenance plants needed for ecological restoration across the country.

blocks.heading: Seed collection: a critical first step
blocks.alt: A seed collector gathering seed from a native shrub in the field.
blocks.caption: Seed collection is one of the most important and least visible parts of restoration.

flow.p: Seed collection is one of the most important and least visible parts of restoration.
It involves carefully gathering seed from native plants in the wild to ensure:

ul: genetic diversity is maintained
local ecosystems are properly represented
rare and threatened species can be propagated
restoration plantings are suited to the landscapes they return to

flow.p: Ethical seed collection takes planning, expertise and patience. It requires working with seasons, understanding plant lifecycles, and collecting in ways that protect wild populations.
Within the Landscape Resilience Program, increasing the volume, diversity and access to native seedstock is a key priority for long-term ecological recovery.
Trees For Life plays a vital role in making this possible.

blocks.heading: Trees For Life: expertise, community, and local impact
blocks.alt: Volunteers working together on a Trees For Life planting site.
blocks.caption: Trees For Life has worked for decades to restore South Australia’s landscapes through seed-based restoration, nursery propagation, and hands-on community action.

flow.p: Trees For Life has worked for decades to restore South Australia’s landscapes through seed-based restoration, nursery propagation, and hands-on community action.

A cornerstone of their work is their commitment to seed collection and local provenance, ensuring restoration projects do not just plant more vegetation, but restore ecosystems that truly belong to place.
This approach supports stronger habitats, healthier biodiversity, and better long-term outcomes for wildlife.

flow.h: A nursery growing biodiversity, species by species

flow.p: At the heart of Trees For Life’s impact is their remarkable nursery.

Each year, Trees For Life grows more than 300 different indigenous species of trees, shrubs, grasses and groundcovers. This diversity is essential for restoring functioning ecosystems, not just planting trees.
Unlike many commercial nurseries, Trees For Life is prepared to invest in:

ul: locally sourced provenance seed
hard-to-grow native species
specialised restoration orders
ecological outcomes over convenience

flow.p: Their plants are grown, propagated and nurtured by experienced nursery staff, alongside the support of volunteers who give their time to help restore the landscapes they care about.
This kind of capacity is critical to meeting Australia’s restoration needs.

Our Landscape Resilience Program works directly with existing nurseries and supports the establishment of new hubs to increase the number of plants and species that can be grown for restoration projects.
Trees For Life is a leading example of what this looks like in practice.

blocks.heading: A shared role in the Landscape Resilience Program
blocks.alt: Newly planted native seedlings taking hold in a restored landscape.
blocks.caption: Our Landscape Resilience Program is a national effort to restore ecosystems in climate-impacted and degraded landscapes, improving resilience where it is needed most.

flow.p: Our Landscape Resilience Program is a national effort to restore ecosystems in climate-impacted and degraded landscapes, improving resilience where it is needed most.
The program brings together community nurseries, seed collection initiatives, restoration partners and volunteers to strengthen the restoration supply chain and help landscapes recover.
Through our partnership with Trees For Life, we are helping support the growing and planting of native vegetation that will:

ul: rebuild habitat after disturbance
strengthen biodiversity in high-risk landscapes
restore ecological connectivity
support wildlife and communities into the future

flow.p: This work is practical, long-term, and deeply place-based.
It starts with seed, and it continues through the care, knowledge and effort of organisations like Trees For Life.

flow.h: Working together to restore what has been lost

flow.p: You can be part of this effort too.
When you donate a tree, you help grow and plant native species where they are needed most, supporting the recovery of landscapes impacted by fire, flood and climate extremes.
Your gift contributes directly to our goal of planting 9 million trees by 2030, helping restore habitat, reconnect ecosystems, and give wildlife the space to return.
Every tree begins with a seed, and every donation helps that seed become something lasting.
