title: A New Future for Mundoo Island and the Coorong
standfirst: At The Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife, we are proud to have partnered with the Australian Government and the South Australian Government to support the acquisition of Mundoo Island Station, a 1,900-hectare property at the Murray Mouth that will now be incorporated into Coorong National Park.
hero_alt: Aerial view of Mundoo Island and the channels of the Murray Mouth.
description: The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife has helped secure Mundoo Island Station, a 1,900-hectare property at the Murray Mouth, for addition to Coorong National Park. The acquisition brings Ewe Island, Long Island and surrounding islands into the National Park estate.

flow.p: At The Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife, we are proud to have partnered with the Australian Government and the South Australian Government to support the acquisition of Mundoo Island Station, a 1,900-hectare property at the Murray Mouth that will now be incorporated into Coorong National Park.

This outcome significantly strengthens one of Australia’s most important wetland landscapes by bringing Mundoo Island, together with Ewe Island, Long Island and surrounding smaller islands, into the National Park estate, and incorporating Lawari Conservation Park into Coorong National Park. The acquisition enhances environmental protection across a landscape of profound ecological and cultural value.

We are honoured to have contributed to this outcome alongside our partners, including the Ngarrindjeri Aboriginal Corporation, local communities and environmental agencies. This collaborative approach reflects a shared commitment to caring for Country, restoring natural systems and protecting vital habitat.

blocks.heading: What Makes Mundoo Island So Significant?
blocks.alt: Aerial view of Mundoo Island's wetlands and shallow channels.
blocks.caption: Mundoo Island sits within the Ramsar-listed Coorong and Lakes Alexandrina and Albert Wetland, an internationally recognised ecosystem that supports migratory shorebirds, threatened wetland species and unique estuarine habitats.

flow.p: Mundoo Island sits within the Ramsar-listed Coorong and Lakes Alexandrina and Albert Wetland, an internationally recognised ecosystem that supports migratory shorebirds, threatened wetland species and unique estuarine habitats. Transitioning the island from pastoral land to National Park management creates an opportunity for the landscape to recover, regenerate and return to a healthier ecological state, supporting species that depend on this fragile environment.
The acquisition strengthens environmental resilience across the Murray Mouth and Coorong, reconnecting habitat, supporting water quality and improving biodiversity outcomes over the long term.

blocks.heading: What National Park Protection Means for the Landscape
blocks.alt: Saltmarsh and native vegetation on the island seen from the air.
blocks.caption: With Mundoo Island now transitioning into Coorong National Park, the focus moves from agricultural use to long-term ecological restoration and land stewardship.

flow.p: With Mundoo Island now transitioning into Coorong National Park, the focus moves from agricultural use to long-term ecological restoration and land stewardship. National Park status ensures wetlands, saltmarshes and native vegetation can regenerate under science-informed management, and that Aboriginal heritage and cultural sites are formally recognised and protected.
The Minister for Climate, Environment and Wate, Lucy Hood emphasised the significance of this transition, stating:

“More habitat will be provided, and protected, for key fish and bird species that attract visitors with spectacular displays. By transforming this site, we have moved to improve environmental resilience, reduce nutrient input and boost water quality.”
A new management plan will bring together conservation priorities, cultural values and community partnership to guide the future of the site.

flow.h: A Place of Deep Cultural Connection

flow.p: Mundoo Island holds deep cultural and spiritual significance for the Ngarrindjeri people, whose connection to this landscape extends across thousands of years. The acquisition strengthens First Nations leadership in land stewardship and protects cultural places, stories and knowledge embedded in Country.

“Ngarrindjeri Aboriginal Corporation look forward to working in co-partnership relationship with the State Government around the care and protection of Mundoo Island into the future,” said Ngarrindjeri Aboriginal Corporation Executive Officer Bill Wilson.
We are committed to supporting an outcome that places cultural care and ecological protection side-by-side.

blocks.heading: Benefits for Land, Wildlife and Community
blocks.alt: Shallow water and sandbars where shorebirds feed near the Murray Mouth.
blocks.caption: The protection of Mundoo Island will deliver lasting benefits for both nature and people.

flow.p: The protection of Mundoo Island will deliver lasting benefits for both nature and people. Restoring wetland ecosystems will improve landscape health and strengthen ecological connections across the region. For wildlife, particularly threatened and migratory shorebirds such as the curlew sandpiper, banded stilt and red-capped plover, the recovery of feeding and nesting habitat is critical to supporting declining populations.
This acquisition also contributes to national conservation priorities, including progress toward protecting 30 per cent of Australia’s land by 2030.
FNPW CEO Ian Darbyshire reflected on the significance of the partnership, stating:

“The acquisition of Mundoo Island Station marks a significant milestone in the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife’s commitment to safeguarding Australia’s unique natural environment and protecting First Nations cultural heritage.”

“We are proud to partner with the Australian and state governments to support the conservation of up to 65 nationally listed threatened species and three threatened ecological communities, helping to set a global benchmark for conservation excellence.”

flow.h: Working Together for the Future of this Landscape

flow.p: The acquisition of Mundoo Island demonstrates what is possible when governments, Traditional Owners, communities and conservation partners work together to protect landscapes of irreplaceable environmental and cultural value.

At FNPW, we are delighted to have played a role in this historic outcome and remains committed to supporting projects that restore ecosystems, protect threatened species and honour the deep relationship between people, culture and the natural world.

title: Caring for Country Starts with Listening
standfirst: Before the first seed goes in the ground, before volunteers gather at the edge of a paddock, before we talk about what a healthy landscape looks like, there’s a conversation that has to happen first. And it starts with listening.
hero_alt: Kaurna practitioners caring for Country on Kaurna Yarta
description: Our partnership with Kaurna Kardla on Kaurna Yarta begins before any planting does. Kaurna knowledge holders on how Country is read, what healthy Country looks like, and what listening makes possible.
credit: With thanks to Kaurna Kardla, the Kaurna community and Firesticks. Written contributions by Michele Simpson, Kaurna woman.

flow.p: Before the first seed goes in the ground, before volunteers gather at the edge of a paddock, before we talk about what a healthy landscape looks like, there’s a conversation that has to happen first. And it starts with listening.
This is the foundation of our partnership with Kaurna Kardla on Kaurna Yarta, the Country of the Kaurna Miyurna — the original people of Adelaide and the Adelaide Plains.

For over 60,000 years, Kaurna Miyurna read this Country. They understood its seasonal rhythms, the way water moved through its creek beds and coastal plains, the moment when conditions were right to burn and when they were not. That knowledge did not disappear. But for generations, it was not being applied to the land.
Restoring that connection is not something that begins with an action plan. It begins with sitting down, paying attention, and learning how to listen.

flow.h: The Knowledge is in the Landscape

flow.p: Kaurna custodians have long held a sophisticated understanding of this Country, a knowledge system that is living, relational, and fundamentally ecological. Their practice of kardla purtulto purunna (fire stick farming) combined deep knowledge of seasonal systems, wind patterns, the life cycles of animals and plants, and the behaviour of water in the landscape.
Decisions about when to burn, where to burn, and how to burn were guided by what the Country was telling them. The land itself was, and still is, a teacher.
“The knowledge is in the landscape. The Elders have not passed. The land is an Elder too.”
Victor Steffensen, Tagalaka man and Firesticks Co-founder

flow.h: Reading Country: What Kaurna Knowledge Tells Us About When, Where and How
Seasonal and ecological indicators for Cultural Burning on Kaurna Yarta

flow.p: On Kaurna Yarta (Country across the Adelaide Plains and surrounding regions), cultural burning is guided through a holistic understanding of Country and its seasonal rhythms rather than fixed schedules.

Decisions around burning are informed by the condition and health of the landscape, including plants, animals, soils, and water systems, with careful attention to how ecosystems are responding at a given time.

This approach reflects a broader and wholistic cultural practice of working with Yarta in a way that supports regeneration, protects biodiversity, and maintains ecological balance. Burning is therefore undertaken when conditions are considered appropriate for sustaining the long-term health and resilience of the environment.

flow.h: How Kaurna practitioners “read” the land before burning

flow.p: Reading the land within cultural burning practices involves understanding Yarta as an interconnected system, where decisions are shaped by long-term observation, experience, and cultural knowledge.

Practitioners consider the overall health and condition of the landscape, including vegetation, waterways, landforms, and the broader ecological balance, to determine how fire may support regeneration and care for Yarta.

This knowledge is grounded in teachings passed through generations and reflects a place-based approach to land management. Cultural authority and ecological understanding guide where and how fire is used, recognising that some areas require protection or different forms of care due to their environmental or cultural significance.

flow.h: What healthy Kaurna Country looks like

flow.p: Healthy Kaurna Yarta is often described as open, diverse, and balanced. Native grasses, herbs, and shrubs coexist in a mosaic pattern rather than forming dense, uniform stands. There is space to move through the landscape, and a visible layering of plant life supports different species.

Biodiversity is a key indicator, birds, insects, reptiles, and mammals are present and active. Soil is stable and rich, not compacted or eroded, and waterways are functioning with good flow and vegetation along their edges.
Cultural Fire aims to restore and maintain this condition.

flow.h: Culturally significant sites, species, and landscape features

flow.p: On Kaurna Yarta, certain sites carry deep cultural meaning and are treated with care. These can include ceremonial places, burial sites, scar trees, and areas associated with Dreaming stories.
Such places may be excluded from burning or managed in very specific ways.

flow.h: What it means to “listen to Country” in a Kaurna context

flow.p: Listening to Country is both practical and deeply cultural. It means observing with patience, watching seasonal shifts, noticing subtle changes in plant and animal life, and responding rather than imposing.

It also involves respecting knowledge held by Elders and community, and understanding that Country communicates through patterns, cycles, and relationships. Fire is not used as a blunt tool but as part of an ongoing relationship with the land.

Listening means knowing when not to burn as much as when to burn. It reflects a responsibility to care for Country in a way that sustains its health, honours its cultural significance, and ensures its vitality for future generations.

In May 2021, a Cultural Burn took place in the Adelaide Park Lands. It was the first on Kaurna Yarta since colonisation. Carried out in partnership with the City of Adelaide, Green Adelaide, and the Kaurna community under the name Kaurna Kardla Parranthi, it was a landmark moment ecologically, and culturally.

Kaurna Kardla grew from Kaurna community leadership and a long-standing commitment to caring for Kaurna Country through Cultural Fire. Since 2019, Kaurna practitioners have strengthened Cultural Fire practice through workshops and on-Country work led by Kaurna authority, supported by Firesticks. Over time, this support helped build skills, systems, partnerships, and confidence, enabling the Kaurna Fire Team to expand its workforce, deliver Cultural Fire programs, and ultimately establish Kaurna Kardla Ltd as an autonomous Kaurna-led organisation in 2026. Today, Kaurna Kardla continues this work independently, grounded in Country, culture, and Kaurna decision-making.

This is what our partnership with Kaurna Kardla is built on. We’re working with these communities, following the lead of knowledge holders, supporting what they know needs to happen, and being patient enough to let that process take the time it requires.

flow.h: Workshops, Volunteers, and the Work of Partnership

flow.p: For more than a decade, Firesticks has walked alongside communities to revitalise Cultural Fire practice and strengthen the knowledge systems that sustain healthy Country and resilient futures. Since 2020, Firesticks has facilitated more than 300 Indigenous Land Management workshops across Australia, supported over 750 Indigenous community members to learn Traditional Land Management practices, and built partnerships with more than 20 councils, ranger groups, land councils, and industry bodies.

The workshops are where knowledge meets practice. Where Elders and young people stand on the same ground together. Where volunteers (Indigenous and non-Indigenous) learn not just a technique, but a way of seeing Country. As Kaurna Ngarrindjeri Cultural Bearer Allan Sumner has said of the fire and smoke that connects Kaurna people back to Country: it’s not just ecological. It activates something in people.

Our volunteers play a real role in this work. But their role is shaped by what knowledge holders determine is appropriate, not the other way around. Before a volunteer holds a tool or sets foot on site, introductions are made, context is given, and the cultural authority guiding the day is established. This is not bureaucracy. It is respect.

flow.h: Indigenous Communities Speaking to Each Other

flow.p: One of the most important, and least visible parts of this work is what happens between Indigenous communities themselves.

Firesticks have facilitated international knowledge exchanges and national gatherings that bring Indigenous practitioners together to share methods, observations, and understanding across cultural boundaries. These are practitioner-to-practitioner conversations, on their terms, about what their Country needs.
“This program brought us together as a community to work together. We’re not just caring for Country, but caring for each other.”
Brad Moore, Senior Land Services Officer, Greater Sydney Local Land Services

When communities share knowledge across regions and nations, practices that may have been suppressed or lost in one place can be rekindled through the experience of another. This is cultural continuity as a living, networked process, not a single, isolated act of revival.
There is a pattern that shows up consistently in genuine partnerships between Indigenous communities and non-Indigenous organisations. And it doesn’t begin with activity. It begins with listening.

Listening means creating space, not just time on the calendar, but genuine willingness to receive knowledge that may challenge assumptions about how land should be managed, what results should look like, and who gets to determine what “healthy Country” means.

Dadirri is an Indigenous concept, rooted in Ngangiwumirr culture and described by Miriam Rose Ungunmerr as an inner, deep listening, a quiet stillness that is the precondition for real relationship. Elder and academic Judy Atkinson connects it directly to trust:
“We first need to listen quietly, in order to gain trust and respect. I will listen to you, share with you, as you listen to, share with me.”
Judy Atkinson, Aboriginal Elder and academic

This sequencing matters. Understanding doesn’t happen because information was transferred. It happens because a relationship was built patiently enough that knowledge could be shared safely. And trust — real, durable trust — is what grows from that understanding. Not from a signed partnership agreement. Not from a single workshop day. From time, from showing up, from following through, and from accepting that the pace of this work is set by the community, not the project timeline.
This is a long way from how much of conservation has historically operated. And it is exactly where FNPW is committed to doing things differently.

flow.h: What Listening Has Made Possible on Kaurna Yarta

ul: A specific moment or observation from a burn or workshop that illustrated the power of following Country’s lead

flow.p: There was a moment in the afternoon during one of our burns where I was sitting on the hillside with our team and stakeholders while we waited for the burns to settle. In this quiet moment, the conversation shifted towards a topic of immense importance: men’s mental health.

It was profound to witness how the act of coming together on Country, engaging in cultural practices, and sharing our experiences not only provided an environment of support and understanding but also highlighted the healing power of connection to land and community.
As a Kaurna woman, as a daughter, sister, aunt and friend I listened quietly and was deeply proud. In that moment, Country held us, and in being held, people felt free to share.

It was a powerful reminder that cultural practice is never just about land management. The act of caring for Country calls something out of us. It reconnects us to each other, to our responsibilities, and to ourselves.
When we tend to Country, Country tends to us in return and by healing Country, we heal ourselves and the relationships that hold our communities together.
Written by Michele Simpson. Kaurna woman

ul: How the relationship between Kaurna practitioners and non-Aboriginal partners has changed the quality of the work over time

flow.p: Over time, the relationship between Kaurna practitioners and non-Aboriginal partners has strengthened through greater trust, respect, and recognition of Kaurna cultural authority on Country. As partnerships have evolved, there has been a growing understanding that cultural burning is not only a land management practice, but also a cultural responsibility connected to identity, knowledge, and ongoing care for Country.

This shift has improved the quality of the work by creating more collaborative and culturally informed approaches. Non-Aboriginal partners have increasingly recognised the importance of listening to and learning from Kaurna Elders and knowledge holders, allowing projects to be guided and led by local cultural values alongside ecological objectives.

As relationships deepen, there is often greater space for shared learning, long-term planning, and mutual accountability. This has supported stronger outcomes for Country, while also contributing to cultural renewal, knowledge sharing, and the rebuilding of practices that were historically disrupted through colonisation.

ul: What becomes possible when volunteers and land managers genuinely listen, rather than arrive with pre-set expectations

flow.p: When volunteers and land managers approach Country with openness and a willingness to genuinely listen, different kinds of relationships and outcomes become possible. Listening creates space for Kaurna cultural knowledge, lived experience, and deep connections to Country to guide the work, rather than being treated as secondary to external systems.

This approach encourages collaboration built on respect, reciprocity, and shared responsibility for caring for Country. Instead of imposing predetermined ideas, people become more attentive to what the landscape, community, and cultural knowledge holders are communicating about what is needed in a particular place.

Through this process, partnerships can move beyond transactional engagement toward more meaningful and culturally safe ways of working together. It allows for stronger trust, deeper learning, and more responsive land management practices that recognise Country as living, interconnected, and deserving of care grounded in relationship rather than control.

ul: Anything Kaurna knowledge holders want to say directly about what listening means in this context

flow.p: Listening requires a willingness to slow down and learn without assuming authority or immediate understanding. It involves creating space for Kaurna voices to lead conversations about Country and acknowledging that meaningful collaboration comes from trust built over time, not from predetermined outcomes.

Importantly, listening is reflected through actions as much as words. It is demonstrated when people remain open to changing their approaches, respecting cultural protocols, and supporting ways of caring for Country that are guided by Kaurna knowledge, values and ongoing connection to place.

flow.h: The Land Does Not Wait, But It Does Reward Patience

flow.p: Allan Sumner, Kaurna Ngarrindjeri Cultural Bearer, said of the first Cultural Burn in Adelaide’s Park Lands: “It’ll awaken those seeds that have been lying in the ground for many years.”

That word: awaken, is the right one. The seeds have been there. The knowledge has been there. The Country has not forgotten what it needs. What has been absent is the practice, and the conditions — cultural, relational, political — that allow that practice to return.
Those conditions are not created quickly. But when they are, when the right listening has happened, when trust has been built between people and between people and Country, the land responds.
This is what FNPW is supporting on Kaurna Yarta, alongside Firesticks and the Kaurna community. Not a program with a fixed endpoint, but a relationship with a long horizon.

We acknowledge the support of Firesticks, who provided wraparound assistance over three years to support Kaurna leadership in reclaiming and strengthening Cultural Fire practice, and in building organisational, enterprise, and governance capability toward autonomy. Today, Kaurna Kardla Ltd stands as an autonomous, Kaurna-led organisation.
FNPW is proud to support Firesticks and the Kaurna community in their work to restore Cultural Fire and land management practices on Kaurna Yarta.

title: Caring for Country in Practice with Firesticks
standfirst: Indigenous Land Management at Field River
hero_alt: The Field River valley at Hallett Cove, with open grassy slopes and scattered trees.
description: At Field River in Hallett Cove, the Kaurna Firesticks team is caring for Country with Cultural Fire, weed control and ecological restoration. The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife supports the work, with Kaurna leadership at its centre.

flow.h: Indigenous Land Management at Field River

flow.p: At Field River in Hallett Cove, the land tells a long story.

The river runs west from the southern Mount Lofty Ranges to the Gulf St Vincent, cutting through steep rocky valleys and open grassy slopes before meeting the sea. Today it sits within suburban Adelaide, bordered by homes, roads and walking tracks. Visitors come for coastal views and open space. But for Kaurna people, this is Kaurna Yarta. It is Country with living cultural memory.
On this landscape, the Kaurna (Kauwi-marnirla) Land Management team at Firesticks is working on Country again.

This work is practical, on-ground Indigenous land management in action. Cultural Fire, ecological restoration, weed control, seasonal observation and community engagement are all part of daily practice. It is about restoring relationship as much as restoring landscape.

flow.h: Igniting Kaurna Cultural Understanding for All

flow.p: The program at Field River, Igniting Kaurna Cultural Understanding for All, supports the Kaurna Firesticks Team to strengthen their knowledge, skills and reach. It builds on the broader strategy of Reigniting Kaurna Cultural Practices Through Fire and is delivered in partnership with Firesticks, Green Adelaide, National Parks and Wildlife Service and local councils.
The team at FNPW plays a supporting role, helping connect partners, secure resources and ensure that Kaurna leadership remains at the centre of the work.
Rayne Simpson, a Kaurna and Narungga man and Regional Coordinator with Firesticks, describes the approach:
“On Kaurna Yarta (Country), caring for land and water means recognising the deep cultural knowledge and responsibility that Kaurna Miyurna (People) have carried for thousands of years.
I believe that strong land management comes from genuine partnerships with the Kaurna community, where Traditional Owners guide how Yarta is cared for and their voices are central in decision-making.
By working together and respecting Kaurna knowledge, culture, and connection to Yarta, we can support healthier landscapes, protect cultural heritage, and build a shared future.”
At Field River, you can see that philosophy in action. The Kaurna Firesticks Team are leading land management work, on their own Country.

flow.h: Indigenous Land Management as a Living System

flow.p: Indigenous land management is often misunderstood as a single practice, most commonly Cultural Burning. In reality, it is a holistic system of care.

Land, water, fire, plants, animals and people are interconnected. Cultural Lore guides how and when to act. Deep seasonal observation informs decisions. The aim is not short-term intervention but long-term balance.

At Field River, the restoration vision recognises that before colonisation, this landscape was an open grassy woodland system. Grasses and low understorey species were maintained through regular Cultural Fire. These open systems supported biodiversity and allowed for movement, visibility and safety.

Following colonisation, agricultural clearing, grazing and later urban development disrupted these processes. When livestock were removed in the 1990s, woody weeds such as olives expanded rapidly. The absence of regular, low-intensity fire changed fuel structure and increased ecological imbalance.

Indigenous land management responds to these changes in an integrated way. Managing fuel is not separate from managing biodiversity. Water systems are not separate from plant communities. Cultural heritage is not separate from ecological health.
Each decision is made in relationship with Country.

flow.h: Cultural Fire Within the Broader Practice

flow.p: Cultural Fire is one tool within this broader system.

It differs fundamentally from conventional hazard reduction burning. Cultural Burning is applied at the right time, in the right conditions, informed by seasonal indicators, plant responses and knowledge held by Traditional Owners. It’s not simply about reducing fuel loads. It’s about promoting regeneration, encouraging specific species, and protecting cultural sites.

At Field River, Cultural Fire sits alongside targeted woody weed control and ecological restoration works. Together, these actions reduce extreme fuel loads while also supporting native grasslands and culturally significant plant communities.
Fire is guided by relationship, not solely by prescription.

flow.h: Why This Matters in an Urban Landscape

flow.p: Field River sits within metropolitan Adelaide. Suburbs such as Hallett Cove and Sheidow Park surround the valley. Visitor numbers are high, particularly during warmer months. Built assets, walking trails and adjacent residential areas increase the complexity of land management.
Historical fire management planning in the southern foothills has identified high fuel levels and the risks associated with urban interface landscapes
The Field River Restoration Plan similarly emphasises the importance of restoring ecological processes while protecting life and property.
Aboriginal land management offers a proactive pathway to resilience.

Rather than responding only when conditions become extreme, cultural practice seeks to prevent imbalance before disaster occurs. By reintroducing regular, controlled fire and addressing weed-driven fuel accumulation, the Kaurna Firesticks Team is reducing risk while strengthening biodiversity.
Central to this work is governance.

Cultural authority remains with the Kaurna Nation. Knowledge sovereignty is respected. Decisions are guided by Kaurna leadership, supported by Firesticks’ Indigenous governance structures and advisory mechanisms.

Partnerships with Green Adelaide, National Parks and Wildlife Service and other agencies are collaborative, but Kaurna leadership is not diluted within these arrangements. Practice informs policy, not the other way around.

Government agencies are engaged in conversations about how regulatory frameworks can better reflect on-ground Aboriginal land management. This includes acknowledging that traditional fire practice operates within a legal environment that has historically limited Indigenous access to Country.
Transparency and trust are foundational. This is long-term work that recognises that restoring both landscape and governance takes time.
At Field River, the impacts are already visible.

Fuel loads are being reduced in a way that supports ecological outcomes. Culturally significant areas are being protected. Young Kaurna people are gaining employment, skills and pathways into leadership. The broader community is learning that Aboriginal land management is not historical knowledge, but contemporary practice.
The Field River Restoration Project recognises that landscape recovery is a multi-decade process. Cultural revival operates on a similar timescale.
This work builds resilience at multiple levels: ecological, cultural, social and institutional.

Caring for Country is not an abstract concept at Field River. It is active, practical and grounded in place. It is Kaurna people working on Kaurna Yarta, supported by partners who recognise that meaningful change happens when Traditional Owners lead the care of their own lands.
In the heart of urban Adelaide, that leadership is reshaping how land management is understood and practiced.

title: The science of plant selection, and why the species matters
standfirst: Who are you planting it for?
hero_alt: Native plantings in a restoration site, chosen for the species that depend on them
description: Put a Glossy Black-Cockatoo in a healthy forest and it can still starve. Why the species list, the seed source and the genetic spread decide whether a planting becomes habitat.

flow.h: Who are you planting it for?

flow.p: Put a Glossy Black-Cockatoo in a healthy forest and it can still starve.
Not because the forest is degraded. Because it is the wrong forest.

Last time we wrote that a bush is a building, and that its structure matters more than its tree count. This is the part where you decide who moves in. Because “we planted a bunch of trees ” is a volume statistic. The ecological question is narrower, and much harder. Which trees, and for whom.

flow.h: One bird, two trees, no substitutes

blocks.alt: glossy black cockatoo

flow.p: The South Australian Glossy Black-Cockatoo feeds almost exclusively on the seed of the drooping sheoak, Allocasuarina verticillata. Not sheoaks in general. That one. And it does not forage evenly across the trees available to it either. Researchers on Kangaroo Island have spent years working out which cone and tree characteristics decide where these birds will and will not feed.
Then there is the second requirement, and it has nothing to do with food. Glossies nest in hollows, in large old eucalypts.

So the bird needs two entirely unrelated species, delivering two entirely different things, on two entirely different timelines. Plant only sheoaks and you have fed a bird that cannot breed. Plant only eucalypts and you have housed a bird that cannot eat. Plant both this decade and the food arrives in years, while the nest sites arrive next century.

The South Australian population climbed from 158 birds in 1995 to around 453 by 2023, which is a genuine recovery story. Then the Black Summer fires destroyed at least 54 per cent of their feeding habitat and 38.5 per cent of known nests in a single season.
That is what a species list is really deciding.

blocks.alt: regent honey eater

flow.p: Fewer than 400 Regent Honeyeaters remain in the wild. They are critically endangered, they depend on flowering eucalypts, particularly yellow box and mugga ironbark, and they range across more than half a million square kilometres chasing blossom.

They have to, because eucalypts are unreliable. Flowering is irregular, heavy in some years and absent in others, and it varies between individual trees in the same stand. A nectar feeder cannot settle down. It follows the food or it does not eat.

Which means a species list is not only what you plant. It is when those plants flower. A revegetation site that blooms gloriously in spring and offers nothing in July is a feast followed by a famine, and the famine is the part that decides whether anything stays.

flow.h: Sometimes the plant is not the food

flow.p: At Winton Wetlands in Victoria, we funded the translocation of around 60 Growling Grass Frogs to establish a new population, in a targeted recovery plan.

Frogs do not eat the vegetation. They need it for something else entirely. Growling Grass Frogs require cover in and around the water, and they also need to bask. Raising their body temperature helps them resist chytrid fungus, the disease behind amphibian collapses worldwide. So habitat work for this species means planting for shelter while deliberately leaving open, sunlit places to warm up in, and adding rock.
Same principle, completely different logic. Here the vegetation is chosen for what it physically does, not for what it feeds.

flow.h: A thousand plants can be one plant

flow.p: Here is the part almost nobody outside the sector thinks about.

Collect seed from three convenient trees, grow a thousand seedlings, and you have not planted a thousand plants. You have planted a very small number of plants, a thousand times over. The genetic variation that lets a population survive drought, disease and heat is simply not in the box.

And it gets worse in exactly the places restoration tends to happen. Small, isolated remnants produce less seed, of poorer quality, with narrower genetic diversity, because the plants that remain are increasingly related to each other. A landmark Australian paper by Broadhurst and colleagues concluded that the emphasis on strictly local seed sourcing will, in many cases, lead to poor restoration outcomes, and argued for concentrating less on how local the seed is and more on how genetically diverse and high quality it is.

This is why “locally sourced” in our reporting means seed collected across many parent plants, not simply seed collected nearby. It is also why community nurseries and seedbanks are infrastructure rather than sentiment.

flow.h: Planting for a climate that has not arrived yet

flow.p: Which brings us to the most interesting unresolved question in Australian restoration right now.

The traditional rule is local provenance. Use seed from as close to the site as possible, because local plants are adapted to local conditions. It is sound logic and it has guided planting for decades.

But the conditions are moving. So Australian researchers have proposed alternatives, most prominently climate-adjusted provenancing, which mixes local seed with seed collected from populations lying in the direction the climate is travelling, typically hotter and drier. The aim is to give a planting the genetic raw material for the climate it will face in fifty years, not only the one it faces today.

Both positions carry real risk. Stay strictly local and you may plant something exquisitely adapted to a climate that is on its way out. Move seed too far and you risk outbreeding depression, where mixing distant populations produces less fit offspring.
There is no settled answer yet, and anyone who tells you there is has stopped reading.

flow.h: Which is why the nursery matters

flow.p: We support community nurseries across four states, with living seedbanks and community groups that tend to them, and we have propagated and planted more than 110,000 fire-resilient natives.

Not because growing plants locally is charming. Because the species list, the seed source and the genetic spread are the three decisions that determine whether a planting becomes habitat, or just becomes trees.
The question is never how many.
It is who are you planting it for.

title: Years of restoration, written in layers
standfirst: A morning in Hindmarsh Valley National Park, where a cleared paddock is becoming a forest again.
hero_alt: Endangered orange daisies flowering in restored ground at Hindmarsh Valley National Park
description: A morning in Hindmarsh Valley National Park, South Australia, where a cleared paddock is becoming a forest again, and why connection matters more than tree counts.
credit: With thanks to Anthony Abley and National Parks and Wildlife South Australia, and to One Tree Planted, whose support funds the plantings described here.

flow.h: A morning in Hindmarsh Valley National Park, where a cleared paddock is becoming a forest again

flow.p: A few years ago, this hillside off Hindmarsh Falls Road was nothing but pasture. Now it has layers: bushes, shrubs and trees taller than a person at the top of the hill, and new seedlings pushing through at knee height behind them. This is a 60 hectare section of Hindmarsh Valley National Park that was only recently brought into the park, and restoration here has been underway for a few years already. With the support of our partners at One Tree Planted, those layers are what years of steady, dedicated work look like on the ground.

We came down to the Fleurieu Peninsula in late May to walk the site with Anthony Abley, the regional ecologist leading this work for National Parks and Wildlife. What he showed us was a work in progress, done paddock by paddock as time and funding allow. You can never do it all at once, he told us, so you do it piece by piece and keep on top of it. But the pieces are starting to join up, and the species are starting to answer.

To understand why this corner of South Australia matters so much, you have to go back millions of years. Hindmarsh Valley, along with the neighbouring Inman and Back Valleys, was shaped by ancient glacial activity. Those old valleys created natural breaks and boundaries that, over an enormous span of time, produced something unusual: a dense pocket of endemic species, plants and animals that live here and nowhere else on earth.

That uniqueness is what makes the work urgent. When a species exists in only one valley, fragmentation is not an inconvenience, but an existential threat. For years, many of these species had been written off, hanging on along roadsides and in scattered remnants. The arrival of this park changed the maths. With 500 hectares now available to restore across the broader Hindmarsh Valley landscape, there is a genuine chance these species can have a future rather than a slow managed decline.

flow.h: From pasture to wet and dry mosaic

flow.p: The restoration here is not simply about putting trees in the ground. It is about rebuilding a whole ecosystem, including the parts you can’t see. The nationally endangered Fleurieu Swamps and their associated woodland are the heart of this site, and recreating them means recreating the way water moves through the land.

Walk the paddock at the end of winter and you would struggle to cross it without gumboots. It turns to bog. Rather than drain that away, the plan embraces it. The site has been mapped into a patchwork: forest along the watercourses, and discrete swamp patches set into the low, wet ground, each planted with a community of species suited to its conditions. The result, over time, is a gradient of habitat rather than a uniform block of trees, and that structural variety is what wildlife needs.

It is already drawing life back. The native swamp rat, an animal with an unfairly grim name, is one of the gentlest creatures you could hope to meet. Nothing like the introduced black rat, it looks more like a small guinea pig and will often put its paws up on your leg for a sniff before wandering off. Bush rats are turning up too. These small native mammals are a quiet proxy for recovery: when they return, it tells us the food web underneath them is starting to function again.

Some of the most important players here never see daylight. Beneath the soil runs a vast web of fungi, with best estimates suggesting ten times as many fungal species underground as plant species above. Plants and fungi depend on each other, and many native animals feed on the fungi and spread them as they go. When we talk about restoring nutrients to degraded land, this is much of what we mean. You cannot rebuild a forest by planting the canopy alone.

blocks.caption: Connected landscapes around our planting sites.

flow.p: The single most important idea on this site is connection. A patch of habitat on its own, no matter how healthy, can only hold so much. Genetic viability for most species needs something in the order of 500 interconnected individuals, breeding and moving freely across enough habitat to sustain themselves.
In a fragmented landscape, that is almost impossible to achieve.

Rosenberg’s goanna makes the point vividly. It needs roughly 100 hectares per animal, which means this park on its own might support only a handful. The only way to build a viable population is to connect this land to neighbouring parks and willing farmers, stitching the fragments into something whole. By doubling a 200 hectare remnant toward a 500 hectare contiguous patch, we give every species more room, more genetic exchange and more resilience.

Connected, multi-storied habitat does something else too. It gives animals a way to move when conditions turn dangerous. Plantings that include ground shrubs, a mid-storey and a canopy create escape routes through the landscape, koalas using the trees and smaller mammals using the cover below. It is the difference between a population that can survive a disturbance and one that gets wiped out with nowhere to run.

It would be easy to assume the great threat to all this new growth is fire. The reality is more interesting. Many of these species have evolved with fire over millions of years and actually depend on it.

Some plants, including Banksia, need the heat of a burn to release their seed. The danger is not fire itself but fire in a broken landscape, where a single blaze can erase an isolated population with no neighbouring habitat left to recolonise from.

The southern brown bandicoot shows how recovery is supposed to work. When most of the Scott Creek and Mount Bold remnant network burned several years ago, with seventy to eighty per cent lost, the bandicoots vanished from the burnt ground. Within three years they had recolonised most of the burn scar, and within five they were back to pre-fire numbers. That bounce-back only happens when connected habitat sits alongside the burn for animals to shelter in and return from. On this site, the team has even used a prescribed burn to regenerate long-unburnt understorey, because bandicoots favour habitat in that five to fifteen year window after fire. Done well, and increasingly in partnership with First Nations fire knowledge, fire becomes a tool for creating habitat rather than destroying it.

There is a lot of good news threaded through this landscape. The glossy black cockatoo, doing well on nearby Kangaroo Island, is visiting the mainland more and more often, and the answer to keeping it here is gloriously simple: plant a great deal of she-oak for it to feed on. The local bandicoot is the subject of genetic studies likely to confirm it as a species in its own right, distinct from its eastern cousins, with a new name drawn from Aboriginal language, Marti, and the scientific name Isoodon nauticus. Recognising it as its own species means we can protect it properly, and even guide where animals are reintroduced to rebuild the strongest possible populations.

That endangered orange daisy we found flowering through the paddock tells the whole story in miniature. Once locked into the roadsides, it now has a new home in ground that was recently just pasture, coming up everywhere across the restored block. It is no longer hanging on. It is spreading.

Stand on that hillside and look across to the cleared land opposite, and it is not hard to picture what it could become: a forested hill instead of bare ground, a new home for species that have spent decades surviving on the margins. Thanks to the support of partners like One Tree Planted and the people who fund this work, that picture is getting closer paddock by paddock. We intervene where the land needs a hand, and then we let nature do what it has always known how to do. What comes back is more than trees. It is a whole living system, finding its feet again.

title: The Importance of Wildlife Corridors This Summer
standfirst: How connected habitat keeps native animals safer, healthier, and more resilient during Australia’s hottest months
hero_alt: A strip of native vegetation linking two patches of bushland across open country.
description: Connected habitat is what lets native animals find shade, water and a way out of a fire through Australia's hottest months. What corridors do in summer, and how a yard, a balcony or a verge can add to one.

flow.p: Summer in Australia follows a familiar script: climbing temperatures, long dry spells, restless heatwaves, and a rising bushfire threat. For our native wildlife, these conditions can be brutal. When habitat is broken into isolated pockets, animals lose the freedom to move, hide, cool down, and recover.

Wildlife corridors change that. A connected landscape is not just good ecology. It is life support. Corridors help animals escape danger, find food and water, and bounce back after fire or extreme weather. And as summers get hotter, the value of these living pathways rises fast.

blocks.heading: Why Wildlife Corridors matter more in Summer
blocks.alt: A vegetated wildlife corridor running through Tasmanian bushland after fire.
blocks.caption: During heatwaves, animals move instinctively toward shade, water, and cooler pockets in the landscape.

flow.h: Corridors give wildlife options when conditions turn extreme

flow.p: During heatwaves, animals move instinctively toward shade, water, and cooler pockets in the landscape. In heavily cleared or urbanised areas, those options often vanish.
Continuous habitat, even at a small scale, opens safe pathways that let:

ul: Birds move between feeding and watering sites
Lizards and small mammals slip into shaded understorey
Pollinators track flowering resources
Nocturnal species cross open areas without overheating

flow.p: Without these routes, animals can become trapped in baking habitat. Heat stress, dehydration, and reduced survival quickly follow.
Research from CSIRO and the Bushfire and Natural Hazards CRC shows that wildlife corridors:

ul: Offer escape routes during fire
Shelter animals in cooler, damp refuges
Help species return and rebuild after the flames pass

flow.p: Fragmented habitat leaves wildlife cornered with no safe exits. Connected habitat lets animals move around fire fronts and return once conditions settle. Even small plantings along streets or back fences add up, improving the odds of survival when fire strikes.

flow.h: Corridors keep food and water within reach

flow.p: Summer squeezes Australia’s natural food supply. Nectar dries up, insects retreat, seeds drop early, and freshwater shrinks.
Corridors create a chain of microhabitats where wildlife can move between:

ul: Flowering shrubs
Shaded understorey
Water sources
Hollow-bearing trees

flow.p: This mobility is often the difference between making it through the season or not.

flow.h: Landscape elements that contribute to wildlife corridors

flow.p: The diagram below from the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water shows some important landscape elements contributing to wildlife corridors.

blocks.alt: Government diagram showing landscape elements that make up a wildlife corridor, including remnant patches, scattered trees, creek lines and roadside vegetation.
blocks.caption: Diagram: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water.

flow.p: Large reserves matter, but most biodiversity loss happens on private land. That means every backyard, balcony, courtyard, or verge can play a role in stitching fragmented landscapes back together.
Small habitat patches connect into bigger ones. And those networks keep wildlife moving.

flow.h: What you can do in your own yard

ul: Create shade and shelter
Support small birds, skinks, insects, pollinators
Offer privacy and noise buffering
Living trees give food, cover, and nesting space
Safe standing dead trees provide hollows for birds and marsupials
Fallen logs feed fungi and boost soil nutrients

flow.p: Skip the green bin. Instead:

ul: Keep contained compost piles away from fire-prone edges
Encourage the insects and moisture that form microhabitats
Add veg scraps and eggshells to build soil health
Healthy soil leads to stronger plants and better habitat
Low maintenance
Nectar for pollinators
A base layer that supports the whole food web

flow.p: Use tools like the GroNATIVE app, local nurseries, or SEEK / Google Lens to identify local species. Think about the wildlife you love most and plant for them.

ul: Shallow ponds or dishes
Stones or marbles for safe insect landings
Slow-moving water to reduce mosquito risk

blocks.alt: Cockatoos feeding in a suburban backyard planted with native shrubs.

flow.h: If You Don’t Have a Yard

flow.p: You can still help connect the landscape.

ul: Native grasses in pots
Flowering shrubs in containers
Water dishes for birds and insects
Window decals to prevent bird strike
Bee bricks for solitary native bees
Join a community garden
Advocate for native vegetation in local parks
Encourage native plantings in apartment courtyards
Support wildlife-friendly verge projects

flow.p: Each small patch strengthens the bigger network. And that network keeps wildlife breathing, moving, and surviving Australia’s toughest months.

flow.h: How Wildlife Corridors Support Fire Safety

flow.p: Well-designed corridors do more than protect wildlife. They help create safer, more resilient landscapes by:

ul: Slowing wind, which can reduce fire spread
Giving animals safer escape routes
Breaking the landscape into moist, diverse patches that are harder for fire to sweep through
Helping ecosystems recover faster after a burn

flow.p: At the landscape scale, we are already showing what successful wildlife corridors look like through projects such as the Bandicoot Superhighway in South Australia. Delivered in partnership with the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, the Sturt Upper Reaches Landcare Group, the Nature Conservation Society of South Australia and the Australian Government, this community-led effort is reconnecting fragmented habitat for the endangered Southern Brown Bandicoot by creating a safe movement route through the Mount Lofty Ranges.

blocks.alt: A southern brown bandicoot foraging in leaf litter.

flow.p: In just two years, the Bandicoot Superhighway delivered conservation outcomes across 216 hectares of priority habitat, restored and planted 34,699 native seedlings, and brought communities together through workshops, planting days and presentations attended by more than 900 people, including 215 hands-on volunteers.

The project also strengthened scientific knowledge. More than 110 bandicoot sightings were uploaded to a new citizen-science portal, supported by over 800 camera-trapping days across multiple properties. These records confirm how corridors help bandicoots move, forage and survive in increasingly fragmented landscapes.

The benefits reached well beyond ecology. The project invested over $211,000 into local biodiversity work and is projected to generate $1.3 million in economic activity within five years, showing how wildlife corridors support both nature and regional communities.

Working with landholders, partner organisations, community groups and government, we are demonstrating how restoring habitat connections reduces extinction risk, strengthens ecosystems and helps native wildlife move safely across the landscape. These connections matter even more during high-risk summer seasons when linked refuge zones can mean survival.

blocks.heading: A Connected Landscape Is a Resilient Landscape
blocks.alt: A broad band of regrowing rainforest linking forest remnants in the Atherton Tablelands.
blocks.caption: An incredible wildlife corridor north of the Rainforest Rangers working sites in the Atherton Tablelands. Photo credit: Steven Nowakowski

flow.p: Wildlife corridors boost biodiversity, support water and soil health, improve fire resilience, and give native species a real chance in a warming world.

This summer and every summer ahead, the most powerful action we can take is simple: connect the habitat around us. Stitch together yards, balconies, verges, parks, and bushland. Build pathways. Build refuge.
Build a landscape where wildlife has room to move and room to survive.

title: Lesser-Known Endangered Animals, and Why They Matter
standfirst: Some of Australia’s most endangered animals are rarely seen, active at night or hidden within forests, grasslands and wetlands. Their stories aren’t always well known, yet their survival is tightly linked to the health of the landscapes we share.
hero_alt: A pygmy bluetongue lizard at the entrance of a spider burrow in native grassland.
description: Eight endangered Australian animals that rarely make the headlines, from the yellow-bellied glider to the woylie, and what each one does to keep its landscape working.

flow.p: Some of Australia’s most endangered animals are rarely seen, active at night or hidden within forests, grasslands and wetlands. Their stories aren’t always well known, yet their survival is tightly linked to the health of the landscapes we share.

For many species, decline doesn’t happen all at once. It unfolds quietly as habitats fragment, food sources disappear and ecosystems lose their balance. Understanding these animals helps reveal how conservation works best when it focuses on whole landscapes, not just individual species, and why protecting habitat matters now more than ever.
Here are eight endangered Australian animals whose survival is deeply connected to healthy landscapes, functioning ecosystems and thoughtful conservation.

blocks.heading: Yellow-bellied Glider
blocks.alt: A yellow-bellied glider clinging to the trunk of a mature eucalypt at night.
blocks.caption: At night, high in mature eucalypt forests, the yellow-bellied glider launches itself between trees, stretching a velvety membrane from wrist to ankle to glide distances of more than 100 metres.

flow.p: At night, high in mature eucalypt forests, the yellow-bellied glider launches itself between trees, stretching a velvety membrane from wrist to ankle to glide distances of more than 100 metres. From a biomechanical perspective, this membrane (called a patagium) allows the glider to control lift, direction and landing with remarkable precision.

These gliders live in close-knit family groups, sharing large home ranges and denning together in old hollow-bearing trees. They are also among Australia’s most vocal marsupials, producing loud, haunting calls that can carry up to 500 metres through the forest. Scientists believe these calls help maintain territory boundaries and coordinate family members across large forested areas.

Yellow-bellied gliders are part of what ecologists call a sap-feeding guild. They chew distinctive V-shaped notches into tree bark to access sugary sap, a behaviour that also creates feeding sites used by other species. Their dependence on mature forests makes them particularly vulnerable. Logging, land clearing, intense bushfires and the loss of old trees reduce both shelter and food sources, while climate change alters flowering cycles and sap flow.

blocks.heading: Swift Parrot
blocks.alt: A bright green swift parrot perched among eucalypt blossom.
blocks.caption: Bright green and fast-moving, the swift parrot is one of Australia’s most striking birds, and one of its most endangered.

flow.p: Bright green and fast-moving, the swift parrot is one of Australia’s most striking birds, and one of its most endangered. Each year, the entire global population breeds in Tasmania before migrating across Bass Strait to forage along the east coast of mainland Australia.

Swift parrots rely on flowering eucalypts for nectar, particularly blue gums and black gums. When these trees fail to flower, or are cleared, breeding success collapses. The loss of hollow-bearing trees also leaves them vulnerable, as they depend on tree hollows for nesting.

With fewer than a few thousand birds believed to remain, the species faces mounting threats from habitat loss, logging, climate-driven changes to flowering cycles, and predation in nesting areas. Protecting and restoring critical woodland habitat across their migratory range is essential to preventing extinction.

blocks.heading: Northern Hopping-mouse
blocks.alt: A Northern Hopping-mouse on sandy ground, with long hind feet and large ears.
blocks.caption: Once found across northern Australia, the Northern Hopping-mouse is now restricted almost entirely to Groote Eylandt.

flow.p: Once found across northern Australia, the Northern Hopping-mouse is now restricted almost entirely to Groote Eylandt. With oversized hind legs, large eyes and a tufted tail, it is adapted for rapid, energy-efficient movement across sandy soils.

Hopping is not just a quirky trait. From a physiological standpoint, it allows the mouse to travel long distances while conserving energy and reducing contact with hot ground surfaces. This is critical in arid and tropical environments where heat stress can be lethal.

Despite these adaptations, the species has faced relentless pressure from intense fires, habitat disturbance and feral cats. Its disappearance from the mainland in the 1970s highlights how quickly specialised mammals can decline when fire regimes and predator balances are disrupted.
Current conservation efforts focus on fire management, predator control and partnerships with Traditional Owners and local ranger groups, combining cultural knowledge with ecological science.

blocks.heading: Key’s Matchstick Grasshopper
blocks.alt: A small wingless matchstick grasshopper resting on a grass stem.
blocks.caption: Thought to be extinct in Victoria and not seen since the 1960s, endangered Key’s Matchstick Grasshopper was rediscovered in 2018.

flow.p: Thought to be extinct in Victoria and not seen since the 1960s, endangered Key’s Matchstick Grasshopper was rediscovered in 2018.

Small, wingless and easily overlooked, they are a reminder that not all endangered species are large or charismatic. Evolution has shaped this insect for life close to the ground, with limited movement and a strong dependence on specific native grasslands.

Because they cannot fly, populations become genetically isolated when habitat is fragmented. This reduces genetic diversity and resilience, making recovery far more difficult. Since European settlement, more than 96 percent of their range has been lost due to land clearing and overgrazing.

Unlike many insects, these grasshoppers do not die off in winter. This makes them an important food source for birds and reptiles during colder months, when other insects are scarce. Their decline sends ripple effects through the food web.

blocks.heading: Growling Grass Frog
blocks.alt: A growling grass frog half submerged among reeds in still water.
blocks.caption: Named for its deep, growling call, this large frog was once common across south-eastern Australia.

flow.p: Named for its deep, growling call, this large frog was once common across south-eastern Australia. Amphibians like the growling grass frog are considered ecological indicators, meaning their presence (or absence) reflects the health of wetlands.

Growling grass frogs depend on still or slow-moving water with abundant vegetation. Their tadpoles can take up to 15 months to develop, an unusually long period that requires wetlands to persist through multiple seasons.

Habitat loss, altered water flows, disease and introduced predators have driven sharp declines. Because frogs breathe partly through their skin, they are particularly sensitive to changes in water quality, making wetland protection and restoration critical.

blocks.heading: Pygmy Bluetongue Lizard
blocks.alt: A pygmy bluetongue lizard looking out from a spider burrow in native grassland.
blocks.caption: The pygmy bluetongue is one of Australia’s smallest lizards and one of its rarest.

flow.p: The pygmy bluetongue is one of Australia’s smallest lizards and one of its rarest. Measuring just 15 centimetres long, it spends most of its life inside abandoned spider burrows, emerging only to ambush passing insects.

This species is a textbook example of ecological interdependence. It relies on native grasslands, healthy invertebrate populations and the presence of burrowing spiders. If any one of these elements disappears, the lizard disappears with it.

Once thought extinct, the pygmy bluetongue was rediscovered in the 1990s. Today, habitat fragmentation remains its greatest threat, reinforcing how even subtle changes to grassland ecosystems can have permanent consequences.

blocks.heading: Southern Emu-wren
blocks.alt: A Southern Emu-wren perched low in dense heath, its long filamentous tail raised.
blocks.caption: Weighing about as much as a teaspoon of sugar, the Southern Emu-wren is a master of concealment.

flow.p: Weighing about as much as a teaspoon of sugar, the Southern Emu-wren is a master of concealment. Its extraordinary tail, longer than its body and made up of fine filament-like feathers, helps with balance as it moves through dense vegetation.

These birds are weak fliers and spend most of their time running mouse-like through shrubs. This behaviour reduces energy expenditure but comes at a cost: they struggle to cross open or degraded areas.

Several subspecies are now listed as endangered or critically endangered, largely due to habitat fragmentation and fire. Their diet of insects also makes them vulnerable to pesticide use, which can quietly remove a critical food source.

blocks.heading: Woylie (Brush-tailed Bettong)
blocks.alt: A woylie foraging in leaf litter at night, digging with its front feet.
blocks.caption: The woylie is often described by ecologists as an ecosystem engineer.

flow.p: The woylie is often described by ecologists as an ecosystem engineer. As it digs for underground fungi, tubers and roots, it turns over tonnes of soil each year, increasing water infiltration and spreading fungal spores essential for plant growth.
Despite weighing just over a kilogram, a single woylie can move up to six tonnes of soil annually. This soil turnover improves seed germination and helps forests recover after fire.

Once occupying more than half of mainland Australia, woylies are now restricted to small, intensively managed populations. Where foxes and cats are controlled, they recover rapidly, demonstrating how targeted, science-led conservation can restore ecological processes.

flow.h: The Quiet Backbone of Healthy Ecosystems

flow.p: Not all endangered animals are large, charismatic or well known. Many are quiet, hidden or active only at night. Yet each plays a role in keeping ecosystems functioning, from pollination and seed dispersal to soil health and food web stability.
Protecting endangered wildlife means protecting habitats, supporting long-term restoration and recognising that even the smallest species can have an outsized impact on the health of our landscapes.

flow.h: How You Can Help This Christmas

flow.p: Across Australia, many of the species listed here are declining for the same reason: the loss and fragmentation of habitat. Old trees disappear, grasslands shrink, wetlands dry out and forests become harder to move through. When habitat breaks down, wildlife follows.
Through Gift a Tree, you can help change that.

Your gift supports on-ground restoration in high-priority regions, where threatened species are under the greatest pressure and where conservation action can make the biggest difference. By planting native trees and restoring landscapes, we’re rebuilding the food sources, shelter and movement pathways that endangered animals like gliders, parrots, frogs and small mammals rely on to survive.

This Christmas, a Gift a Tree is more than a gesture. It’s a practical way to support endangered wildlife, strengthen ecosystems and help protect Australia’s most vulnerable species where help is needed most.

title: Planning for Fire Season Starts in the Garden
standfirst: As the Australia summer heat starts to build, so does the risk of bushfire, not just in remote forested areas, but around homes, properties and in our wider communities. At the same time, this is a powerful moment for community togetherness, land healing and supporting our native landscapes to recover and thrive. We can work hand-in-hand: preparing our homes, supporting our neighbours, restoring our land.
hero_alt: Australian native bushland and garden vegetation in summer.
description: Bushfire preparation is not only about clearing. Native plants, sensible spacing and connected neighbours all make a place safer, and this guide sets out what to do at home and with your street.

flow.p: As the Australia summer heat starts to build, so does the risk of bushfire, not just in remote forested areas, but around homes, properties and in our wider communities. At the same time, this is a powerful moment for community togetherness, land healing and supporting our native landscapes to recover and thrive. We can work hand-in-hand: preparing our homes, supporting our neighbours, restoring our land.
In this blog we explore:

ul: Why native plants matter in bushfire prevention and land-healing
What you can do at home or as a neighbourhood to make your place safer
How the Fire Wise Project and the Fire Wise Learning Hub offer resources and tools for action

flow.h: Why Native Plants & Smart Vegetation Matter

flow.p: It’s tempting to think that bare ground or removing all vegetation is the safest route when fires loom. But fire science tells us a more nuanced story. Planting native vegetation with the right spacing and plant-types can actually help slow fires and save lives.
Here are a few key scientific points:

ul: Fires move fastest through fine dry fuels like grasses and exposed ground litter, especially when driven by wind.
A moderately dense canopy of native trees/shrubs can provide shade, maintain moist soil, reduce local wind speeds and offer a barrier to ember attack and radiant heat.
After a bushfire, the ecosystem goes through stages of recovery: first colonised by short-lived species that protect soil and provide shelter, then gradually more mature vegetation returns.
Native vegetation isn’t inherently a fire hazard; in fact, with the right design and management, it supports both biodiversity and resilience.

flow.p: So when we think about preparing for summer and restoring our land, the message is: don’t just clear everything, think about strategic planting, nurturing native plants, and working as a community.

flow.h: What You Can Do at Home

flow.p: Here’s a checklist of practical steps you (and your neighbours/community) can take. Adapt them to your context, climate and local native plant list.

flow.h: Secure your property and create defensible space

ul: Remove or regularly clear fine fuels: dry leaves, grass clippings, bark mulch near buildings.
Keep shrubs and trees spaced so fire doesn’t readily climb from ground to canopy.
Prune lower branches of trees to reduce ladder fuels.
Ensure your house/garden access is clear for fire-engine access and evacuation if required.
Make sure your emergency plan is up to date, and your household knows it.

flow.h: Use native plants (and the right ones!)

ul: Choose native plants with lower flammability and plant them in the right locations. The Fire Wise project emphasises the strategic use of native vegetation rather than wholesale clearing.
Use design logic: e.g., waterwise, shade-keeping, windbreaks.
Maintain your plantings: keep them healthy, irrigated (where appropriate), remove dead material.
Consider ground-covers that hold moisture and reduce fine fuels.
Talk with your neighbours: a bushfire-safe community is a connected, informed one. Share ideas, join planting days, form local groups.
Host or attend community native-planting days: these build local ecosystem resilience and social cohesion.
Visit, support or volunteer at local seed banks (native seeds) or community nurseries to grow local plants for fire-wise landscaping.
Share resources and knowledge from the Learning Hub (see below) so everyone is on the same page.

flow.h: After a fire or during recovery

ul: Monitor the site: photograph and revisit. Drops in vegetation or structure need attention.
Control invasive species quickly – they can outcompete native seedlings and create new fuel loads.
Re-plant missing or keystone native species if natural regeneration isn’t sufficient.
Consider cultural burning or Indigenous-led practices if your local context allows, honouring Country and traditional knowledge.

flow.h: The Science + The Community: How They Connect

flow.p: At its heart, fire-prevention and land-healing is both science (fire behaviour, ecology, vegetation management) and community care (neighbours, planting, shared land, Indigenous knowledge). Bridging these gives us real resilience.

For instance: the Fire Wise theory highlights three key fire risks: radiant heat, wind speed and ember attack. By planting the right natives, spaced and maintained, communities can reduce those risks: shade keeps ground moist, trees deflect wind/embers, and healthy vegetation slows flame spread. It’s a simple concept, but when executed across many properties in a neighbourhood, the effect multiplies.

And when a community plants together, shares seeds and knowledge, the social fabric becomes stronger. People know each other, share responsibilities, look out for each other, and that’s another layer of fire safety.
Here are some top resources to help you, your neighbourhood or your organisation get started:

ul: Fire Wise Learning Hub – Explore their learning resources, project case-studies and plant lists. Visit: https://firewisehub.online/
Fire Wise Resources page – https://firewisehub.online/resources/
FNPW Fire Wise Project – https://fnpw.org.au/project/fire-wise/ – gives project overview, science-background, how you can get involved.
Helping the Bush Recover (by Trust for Nature) – Good reading on ecological recovery, timing and weed control. trustfornature.org.au
Practical plant lists & fire-wise landscaping reports (e.g., The Crossing Land’s NSW report) thecrossingland.org.au

flow.p: Tip: Bookmark those URLs, share them in your community newsletter or local social-media group, perhaps even organise a “bushfire-safe native planting” morning.

flow.h: Why It Matters And What’s At Stake

flow.p: When we don’t act, the stakes are high: the 2019-20 “Black Summer” fires illustrated how ecosystems, homes and communities can be devastated. Recovery takes years, biodiversity suffers, and our native species and cultural heritage are under threat.
But when we do act:

ul: Homes become safer
Landscapes become more resilient
Biodiversity is supported
Communities become stronger, connected, proactive

flow.p: And importantly: embracing native species and thoughtful vegetation means we’re healing our land, not just defending it.

This summer, let’s come together: behind our fences, in our streets, in our neighbourhoods. Let’s plant with purpose, look after our native landscapes, and support each other. Fire preparedness it’s about smart design, native planting, shared knowledge and community care.
