title: The Bandicoot: A Little Gardener Beneath Our Feet
standfirst: In the underbrush of Australia’s south and southeast, a small, shy marsupial is quietly performing some of the most important work in our ecosystems. The Southern Brown Bandicoot (Isoodon obesulus) may not have the fame of kangaroos or koalas, but when it comes to ecological impact, this little digger is a heavyweight.
hero_alt: A southern brown bandicoot foraging in leaf litter.
description: One southern brown bandicoot turns close to four tonnes of soil a year, and the Fleurieu Peninsula is one of its last strongholds. Why this shy digger matters, and how the Bandicoot Superhighway is reconnecting its habitat.

flow.p: In the underbrush of Australia’s south and southeast, a small, shy marsupial is quietly performing some of the most important work in our ecosystems. The Southern Brown Bandicoot (Isoodon obesulus) may not have the fame of kangaroos or koalas, but when it comes to ecological impact, this little digger is a heavyweight.

blocks.heading: Meet the Bandicoot
blocks.alt: A southern brown bandicoot moving through a garden bed at dusk.
blocks.caption: This stocky, short-snouted marsupial weighs between 400 grams and 1.2 kilograms, depending on sex and region.

flow.p: This stocky, short-snouted marsupial weighs between 400 grams and 1.2 kilograms, depending on sex and region. It thrives in low scrub, heath, and woodland with dense ground cover. Unlike the tree-dwelling marsupials we often picture, the bandicoot lives on the ground, using its long claws and sharp nose to rummage through leaf litter and soil for invertebrates, fungi, and plant roots.
Rather than simply existing within its habitat, the bandicoot transforms it.

Once a common sight across South Australia, eight species of bandicoot once roamed the state. Today, only the Southern Brown Bandicoot remains. Habitat loss caused by land clearing, infrastructure, and agriculture, along with predation from foxes and cats, has pushed this species onto the Endangered list under the EPBC Act.

Bandicoots rely on dense native undergrowth to hide from predators. As land is fragmented across the Fleurieu Peninsula and Mount Lofty Ranges, many populations have become isolated, unable to move or breed safely between bushland areas.

blocks.heading: Why This Small Creature Matters
blocks.alt: A bandicoot in dense low scrub and heath, its usual habitat.
blocks.caption: The Southern Brown Bandicoot may be small, but it moves an astonishing amount of soil.

flow.p: The Southern Brown Bandicoot may be small, but it moves an astonishing amount of soil. Research in Western Australia’s Yalgorup National Park found that a single bandicoot creates around 45 new foraging pits each day, shifting about 10.7 kilograms of soil daily. That’s nearly 4 tonnes of soil turned over every year by one animal.

This constant digging rejuvenates the earth. Each pit breaks up hardened soil, improves water absorption, and draws buried organic matter to the surface. Studies show that seedlings grown in soil disturbed by bandicoots grow taller, heavier, and faster than those in untouched soil. These little foragers are natural gardeners, physically transforming their environment in ways that help countless other species thrive.

Once widespread across southeastern Australia, the Southern Brown Bandicoot’s range has shrunk dramatically due to habitat clearing and the spread of introduced predators. Genetic studies in South Australia reveal reduced gene flow and greater isolation caused by agriculture and development. Without targeted conservation, scientists predict that up to 84 percent of local populations could disappear within a century. The loss of bandicoots would ripple through the environment, undermining the soil processes that sustain healthy, diverse ecosystems.

Despite these challenges, the Southern Brown Bandicoot shows impressive adaptability. Studies have found that it can survive in modified landscapes, including roadside reserves and drainage channels, as long as there is thick undergrowth and protection from predators. This resilience gives conservationists hope. If habitat corridors, dense vegetation, and predator control are maintained, these remarkable marsupials can continue living alongside us, quietly keeping ecosystems in balance.

blocks.heading: Spotlight: The Bandicoot Superhighway Project
blocks.alt: Volunteers planting native seedlings for the Bandicoot Superhighway project.
blocks.caption: The Bandicoot Superhighway Project, a community-led initiative supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, is helping reconnect fragmented habitats and restore landscapes across South Australia.

flow.p: The Bandicoot Superhighway Project, a community-led initiative supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, is helping reconnect fragmented habitats and restore landscapes across South Australia.
So far, the project has achieved:

ul: 44 hectares of habitat rehabilitation and restoration
34,669 native seedlings planted to rebuild shelter and foraging areas
100+ wildlife cameras installed to monitor local populations
Community workshops empowering residents to protect these important ecosystem engineers

flow.p: By restoring vegetation and improving connectivity across the Fleurieu Peninsula, the project helps bandicoots move freely, breed safely, and continue their crucial role in maintaining soil health. It’s a powerful example of how science, community, and conservation can come together to heal landscapes.

Helping bandicoots helps the land recover. Through community engagement, locals are encouraged to get involved – from tree planting and wildlife monitoring to supporting ongoing restoration through donations.

blocks.heading: How You Can Help
blocks.alt: Volunteers working together on a revegetation site on the Fleurieu Peninsula.
blocks.caption: Bandicoot recovery starts with small actions that add up to big impact.

flow.p: Bandicoot recovery starts with small actions that add up to big impact. You can help protect these unsung heroes by:

ul: Planting or gifting a native tree to restore their habitat. Every native tree contributes to shade, shelter, and insect life that supports bandicoots.
Becoming a Habitat Hero through the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, supporting hands-on conservation work that keeps ecosystems connected.
Keeping cats indoors and dogs on leads in bushland to reduce predation risks.
Reporting sightings to help community monitoring and citizen science programs.

flow.p: Your gifted tree becomes part of a living chain that supports bandicoots, biodiversity, and a healthier Australia.

title: Protecting Australia's Threatened Species
standfirst: Step onto a bush trail at daybreak and you expect the trees to burst with life. Yet across Australia the once bright chorus is fading to a hush. From rainforest canopies to inland salt-marsh, more than 2 000 native species now stand on a cliff edge.
hero_alt: Eucalypt bushland in early morning light.
description: More than 2,000 native species are now listed as threatened. This is what we stand to lose, which animals and plants are closest to the edge, and the work already bringing some of them back.

flow.p: Step onto a bush trail at daybreak and you expect the trees to burst with life. Yet across Australia the once bright chorus is fading to a hush. From rainforest canopies to inland salt-marsh, more than 2 000 native species now stand on a cliff edge.

Many of the voices and colours that once defined our landscapes are fading fast. In this blog, we’ll explore why, spotlight the threatened species in Australia most at risk, and share the hopeful ground-level work already giving them a path back from the brink.

flow.h: Why losing Australia’s threatened species hurts us all

flow.p: Healthy ecosystems quietly keep life humming, often in ways we notice only when something goes wrong:

ul: Pollination and seed dispersal: birds such as the Regent Honeyeater and mammals like the Grey-headed Flying-fox move pollen and seeds across huge distances, supporting crops and regenerating bushland.
Clean water: Murray–Darling river turtles stir sediments, cycle nutrients and keep wetlands clear.
Rich soil: Southern Brown Bandicoots turn over several tonnes of soil each year while foraging, aerating soil and helping leaf litter break down.

flow.p: When these “ecosystem engineers” vanish, services worth billions in agriculture, tourism and disaster resilience begin to unravel.

flow.h: Snapshot of a crisis we can still avert

flow.p: Here’s why urgency matters:

ul: More than 2,000 native species already sit on state or national threatened-species lists.
Koala numbers have fallen by over 50 percent in just two decades.
In parts of the Murray–Darling Basin, nine out of ten river-turtle nests are destroyed each breeding season.
The Regent Honeyeater counts fewer than 300 wild birds, while the Orange-bellied Parrot is down to double digits.

flow.p: Unless we act swiftly, lifelines for many species will close within our lifetime.

blocks.heading: Meet the species on the edge
blocks.alt: Two flying-foxes hanging in the canopy.
blocks.caption: Grey-headed Flying-foxes, among the pollinators and seed couriers now at risk.

flow.p: Regent Honeyeater, Swift Parrot, Orange-bellied Parrot and Grey-headed Flying-fox are vital pollinators and seed couriers, but shrinking old-growth eucalypt woodlands and coastal salt-marsh put them between Endangered and Critically Endangered.

The Murray Short-Necked Turtle has cruised Australian rivers for sixty million years. Today, egg-raiding foxes, hotter summers and flash floods have wiped out up to 90 percent of some local populations.
Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby, Southern Brown Bandicoot and Greater Bilby cling to isolated strongholds, challenged by feral predators and shrinking habitat corridors.
The beloved Koala is now missing from half of its historic range as land clearing, disease and hotter bushfires take their toll.

flow.h: Plants we can’t afford to lose

flow.p: It’s not only animals that are at risk of extinction; rare plants underpin entire food webs.

ul: Kangaroo Island Spider Orchid (Caladenia ovata): a barometer of healthy, species-rich woodlands. After farmland expansion and altered fire patterns, FNPW and local partners are rebuilding the understorey on Kangaroo Island and the Fleurieu Peninsula to help this orchid rebound.

Davidson’s Plum (Davidsonia jerseyana): a nutrient-dense rainforest fruit that feeds birds and supports First Nations enterprises. Northern Rivers nurseries now raise thousands of seedlings for restored creek-line corridors.

Small Purple-pea (Swainsona recta): a bright wildflower that enriches box-gum woodlands by fixing nitrogen. FNPW nurseries in NSW and Victoria propagate plants for return to newly restored woodland plots.

flow.p: When these keystone plants disappear, everything from pollinating insects to seed-dispersing birds feels the loss.

blocks.heading: How we’re turning urgency into action
blocks.alt: A rock-wallaby standing on a rocky outcrop, watching for threats.
blocks.caption: Habitat restoration, nest protection and wildlife corridors, built with Traditional Owners and local communities.

flow.p: At FNPW, we’re working alongside Traditional Owners, researchers, volunteers and local communities to restore habitat, protect nests and rebuild wildlife corridors that can turn the numbers of Australia’s threatened species around.

Thirty community nurseries across four states have produced more than 1 000 000 locally adapted seedlings since 2020, restoring 2 500 ha and reconnecting fragmented corridors rebuild salt-marsh and re-green fire-scarred country, exactly where birds, bats and marsupials need them. With the one millionth tree planted in October 2024, the program now scales toward 8 million trees by 2030.

ul: 1 Million Turtles: Nest guards, wetland repair and hatchling releases lift survival from 10 % in the wild to near 100 % in protected sites.
Nectar Sippers: Flowering eucalypts planted as “stepping-stones” give Regent Honeyeaters and Swift Parrots safe refuelling stops.
Bandicoot Superhighway: In South Australia’s Mt Lofty Ranges, 34 600 native seedlings and habitat works have triggered 110 new Bandicoot sightings in 2023 alone.

flow.h: Conservation Grants and First Nations Partnerships

flow.p: In the Kimberley, Aboriginal rangers from seven language groups use cool patch burning and detailed burrow mapping to protect Greater Bilbies, combining traditional knowledge with modern science.

Since the Black Summer fires, FNPW supporters have helped plant the one-millionth tree for burnt landscapes and restore 2,500 hectares of habitat. 12 nurseries are now growing low-flammability species, and more than 100 landholder workshops now share proven techniques that lower fire risk while boosting biodiversity.

blocks.heading: Proof that hope is justified
blocks.alt: Restored habitat where threatened species are returning.
blocks.caption: Recovery is real.

flow.p: Recovery is real.

ul: Turtles back in the water: school-incubated hatchlings now thrive in revitalised wetlands.
Birdsong returning: new eucalypts in the South-East Woodlands attracted Regent Honeyeaters within just two flowering seasons.
Bilbies on camera: motion-sensor footage shows Bilbies foraging in freshly managed country where cultural burns revived food and shelter.

flow.p: These successes are milestones that prove wildlife rebounds quickly when we give nature a hand.
Volunteer locally
Join tree-planting days, beach clean-ups or citizen-science surveys through our corporate volunteering program.
Give a Gift
Your one-time donation helps drive real, on-the-ground conservation, supporting urgent action for priority projects.
Become a monthly donor
Join Habitat Heroes – a passionate community of monthly givers protecting wildlife all year round.
We put 78% of every dollar straight into field projects, not administration.

ul: $50 plants a tray of native seedlings to rebuild lost habitat.
$100 restores critical woodland or wetland.
$200 funds nest boxes, predator control or Traditional Owner surveys.

flow.p: Envision a dawn where the chorus is strong, rivers run clear and bright wildflowers blanket the ground, an Australia where threatened species not only survive but thrive. By understanding the challenges, celebrating progress and supporting practical on-ground work, we can turn that vision into reality.

title: The Battle in the Treetops: Feathers, Flowers and a Fight for Survival
standfirst: Across Australia’s woodlands, an invisible war is playing out in the treetops.
description: Across Australia’s woodlands, an invisible war is playing out in the treetops.

flow.p: Across Australia’s woodlands, an invisible war is playing out in the treetops.
As eucalypt forests are cleared, fragmented, or weakened by fire and drought, nectar-feeding birds are being forced into tighter and tighter spaces, and some have turned from neighbours into rivals.
What was once a thriving chorus of species now echoes with tension. And it all comes down to the loss of their lifeblood: flowering eucalypts.

flow.h: How Habitat Loss Changed Bird Behaviour

blocks.alt: Australian landscape tree clearing

flow.p: When Europeans arrived, vast grassy woodlands and forests were cleared for livestock, farming, and settlement. The understorey, made up of shrubs, native grasses, and small trees that once sheltered smaller birds, disappeared too.
This shift created the perfect conditions for one species to dominate: the Noisy Miner.

These highly social, aggressive honeyeaters thrive in open, cleared environments where trees stand alone without protective shrub layers. In colonies of hundreds, they fiercely defend their territories, dive-bombing and chasing away any bird that comes too close.
Meanwhile, species that once coexisted peacefully, like the Regent Honeyeater and Swift Parrot, have been pushed to the edge.

blocks.alt: Regent honeyeater bird on branch

flow.p: Once common across the woodlands of south-eastern Australia, the Regent Honeyeater (Anthochaera phrygia) is now critically endangered. These nomadic nectar specialists follow the blooms of eucalypts like Yellow Box, Mugga Ironbark, and Swamp Mahogany, often travelling long distances to find food.
But their feeding grounds have been cut apart by clearing, and the flowering cycles they rely on are increasingly disrupted by climate change and drought.
Now, when they arrive in what should be a rich feeding patch, they are met with an army of Noisy Miners defending every branch.
The result is that the Regent struggles to feed, nest, and breed successfully. Even their nests are torn apart by the miners’ relentless attacks.

blocks.alt: Noisy minor bird sitting in tree on branch

flow.p: The irony is that both the Noisy Miner and the Regent Honeyeater are native species. But human-driven landscape changes have made the Noisy Miner behave much like an invasive one.

Without the dense shrubs that once provided refuge for smaller birds, the miners have spread across farmland, suburbs, and fragmented forests, creating what ecologists call “death zones” or “biological deserts” where almost no other small birds can survive.
Their dominance also sets off a destructive chain reaction:

ul: Fewer bird species means less control of insect populations.
The miners “farm” insects like psyllids, feeding on their sugary secretions (lerp) but not the insects themselves.
As these insects multiply unchecked, they weaken and kill the very eucalypts both species depend on.
Fewer healthy trees mean even less food, and the cycle continues.

blocks.alt: Swift parrots sitting on branch

flow.p:
Another victim of this imbalance is the Swift Parrot, one of only three migratory parrot species in the world.
These striking green and red birds breed in Tasmania, then cross Bass Strait each winter to feed on the same flowering eucalypts as the Regent Honeyeater.
Their threats are twofold: large-scale logging of Tasmanian Blue Gum forests in their breeding grounds, and the competition for dwindling nectar resources on the mainland.
Even more tragically, introduced predators in Tasmania have learned to attack their nests, driving numbers down further.
Short-term solutions like culling Noisy Miners have shown mixed success, as colonies quickly recolonise and the balance rarely lasts.
The true solution lies in restoring diverse, resilient landscapes that support all species.
That means:

ul: Replanting flowering eucalypts and understorey shrubs to provide food and cover.
Protecting mature trees and allowing fallen logs to decompose naturally, enriching soil health.
Supporting Indigenous fire management practices that prevent catastrophic wildfires while maintaining eucalypt regeneration cycles.
Ensuring corridors of connected habitat so birds can move safely and freely between feeding grounds.

flow.p: Through projects like Saving the Nectar Sippers, our organisation and BirdLife Australia are helping replant and reconnect these vital woodland habitats, giving endangered birds like the Regent Honeyeater a fighting chance to recover.

flow.h: Why This Fight for Survival Matters

blocks.alt: blue and yellow bird eating gum leaves

flow.p:
It is easy to think the loss of a few bird species is just nature taking its course.
But every species plays a part in keeping our ecosystems and our lives in balance.

flow.h: Birds Are the Quiet Architects of Our Forests

flow.p: Nectar-feeding birds like the Regent Honeyeater and Swift Parrot are vital pollinators for eucalypts. Each time they dip their curved beaks into a flower, they transfer pollen from one blossom to another, helping trees set seed and regenerate.

Without these birds, many of our most iconic eucalypt species would struggle to reproduce naturally. Over time, that means fewer trees, less shade, weaker soils, and less carbon stored in our landscapes.
Forests and woodlands are not just scenery. They are living infrastructure that keeps our air clean, stabilises our climate, filters water, and supports biodiversity from the canopy to the soil.
The loss of pollinators does not just hurt wildlife, it undermines the ecosystems that sustain human communities.
When trees die and soil degrades:

ul: Erosion increases, silting up rivers and reducing water quality.
Biodiversity declines, which affects natural pest control, seed dispersal, and pollination of crops.
Carbon storage drops, making it harder to slow climate change.
Heat intensifies, because trees regulate temperature and create local cooling effects.

flow.p: These shifts are already affecting rural communities and urban environments across Australia. When landscapes lose their diversity, we lose resilience, the ability of nature to bounce back after fire, flood, or drought.

flow.h: Ecosystems Are Interconnected, Just Like Us

blocks.alt: bee and flower in garden

flow.p: Every living thing in an ecosystem, from the smallest insect to the tallest tree, performs a role that supports the whole.

When one thread is pulled, such as the Regent Honeyeater disappearing from the food web, the entire system begins to fray. The plants it pollinated decline, the insects that relied on those plants vanish, and the soil organisms that depended on their leaf litter weaken. Eventually, even species that seem unrelated are affected.
Humans are not outside this web.
The air we breathe, the food we eat, and the rain that falls all depend on the natural systems that birds quietly help maintain.
Protecting birds is not just about saving wildlife. It is about safeguarding the natural processes that keep Australia alive and thriving.

By restoring woodlands, planting native species, and supporting programs like Saving the Nectar Sippers, we are rebuilding the foundation for a healthier, more resilient planet for every species, including us.

blocks.alt: Planting native australian plants

flow.p: Everyone has a role to play in helping Australia’s birds thrive again. Whether you have a balcony, a backyard, or a whole property, small actions can make a big difference.

ul: Plant native species like grevilleas, bottlebrush, and flowering eucalypts to provide nectar and shelter.
Keep some understorey shrubs because birds need dense areas to nest, rest, and escape predators.
Leave leaf litter and fallen branches to enrich soil and feed insects, which many birds rely on.
Provide water safely with shallow bird baths or small ponds under shade.
Avoid chemical sprays and pesticides, which can harm insects and reduce food sources.
Protect your patch from pets by keeping cats indoors and dogs supervised to help native wildlife survive.

flow.p: If you want to do even more, you can support FNPW’s habitat restoration work.
Make a one-off donation or become a Habitat Hero with a monthly gift to help protect native wildlife year-round.
As a Habitat Hero, you’ll receive inspiring updates about the species and landscapes you’re helping to protect, from eucalypt forests to coastal bushland.

title: Charleston Conservation Park: From Ashes to Banksias
standfirst: When you step into Charleston Conservation Park today, two stories meet your eye. Charred trunks of old banksias still stand from the bushfires of 2019, stark reminders of what was lost. But around them, a new generation of silver banksias is thriving, young trees raised in nurseries and planted by volunteers now bringing the woodland back to life.
hero_alt: silver banksia tree in Charleston Conservation Park South Australia
description: When you step into Charleston Conservation Park today, two stories meet your eye. Charred trunks of old banksias still stand from the bushfires of 2019, stark reminders of what was lost.

flow.p: When you step into Charleston Conservation Park today, two stories meet your eye. Charred trunks of old banksias still stand from the bushfires of 2019, stark reminders of what was lost. But around them, a new generation of silver banksias is thriving, young trees raised in nurseries and planted by volunteers now bringing the woodland back to life.
This is the landscape’s renewal in motion. It’s a story of resilience, of seed saved just in time, and of a community determined to restore one of South Australia’s rarest woodland habitats.

blocks.alt: threatened banksia trees in Charleston Conservation Park South Australia

flow.p: Charleston Conservation Park sits in the Adelaide Hills, just 40 minutes from the city, but it feels a world away. It protects grassy and heathy woodland—manna gums, drooping she-oaks, and most important of all, the silver banksia.
Once common across southern Australia, silver banksias have vanished from much of their range. In South Australia, they hang on in scattered pockets. Charleston is one of their last strongholds.

The park was first proclaimed in 1976 at 54 hectares, and 2017, the park grew by nearly half when an adjoining grazing property was added. The new land was worn down by years of livestock, but it held potential. That same potential made the fire hit even harder.

blocks.alt: Bushfire recovery regrowth in conservation park South Australia

flow.p: n December 2019, the Cudlee Creek bushfire swept through more than 23,000 hectares of the Adelaide Hills. Charleston Conservation Park was caught in the path.

Silver banksias, already hanging on in small numbers, were especially hard hit. Unlike eucalypts, which can resprout, banksias are usually killed outright by intense fire and rely on seed stored in old cones to regenerate. But after years of drought, little viable seed was left on the trees.
What survived was memory, and seed stored in sheds.

Walking through the park now, you can still see the blackened trunks of those lost banksias. But look closer, and you’ll notice rings of young plantings pushing up through the ash, signs of hope rising from devastation.
For years before the fire, a group of locals called the Friends of Charleston Conservation Park had been collecting seed. Quiet work. Careful work. No one knew how urgently it would be needed.
After the fire, that saved seed became a lifeline.

Volunteers, along with Kersbrook Landcare and local nurseries, grew tens of thousands of seedlings. Since 2019, more than 20,000 silver banksias have been planted by hand. That effort is rebuilding an ecosystem from the roots up.

Another 7,500 native plants have gone in too, thanks to support from programs like the Hawke’s Brewing Threatened Species Landcare Grant. Every one of those plants matters – to the woodland birds, to the pygmy possums, to the soil, and to the people who refused to give up.

blocks.alt: Banksia trees in Charleston Conservation Park

flow.p: FNPW’s role has been to support the expansion zone, the eastern half of Charleston added in 2017. This section had been heavily grazed and needed targeted intervention. Through our funding, thousands of plants were grown in nurseries and planted into this area, helping to establish new banksia stands and restore a degraded landscape.
Our focus has been on rebuilding structure and diversity so the park’s woodland can knit back together and provide the food, shelter and resilience wildlife need.

Silver banksias are a keystone species, producing abundant nectar that feeds honeyeaters, insects and even small mammals like the western pygmy possum. Their cones provide seed for birds, while their structure offers shade and shelter for countless creatures. For thousands of years, they also played a role in stabilising soils and supporting the balance of woodland ecosystems across southern Australia.

If silver banksias were to disappear, entire food webs would unravel. The loss of their flowers and seed would ripple across species that depend on them, leaving woodlands weaker and less resilient. Protecting and restoring this species helps ensure that both wildlife and the broader landscape have the resources they need to survive and adapt.

flow.h: Signs of Renewal in Charleston Conservation Park

blocks.alt: South Australia banksia trees after bushfire

flow.p: Today, signs of renewal are everywhere. Kangaroo grass and speargrass tussocks are spreading across the ground layer, holding soil and providing habitat for insects and small reptiles. Honeyeaters dart between young banksias, and robins perch low in the recovering woodland.
The contrast is striking: old, fire-scarred trunks stand side by side with fresh banksia seedlings, living proof that nature, given the right help, can bounce back.

Charleston’s recovery is still a work in progress. Young trees need time to mature, and ongoing challenges like drought, weeds and other impacts of climate change remain. But every new planting strengthens this landscape and every seedling brings back a piece of the woodland puzzle.
With continued care, Charleston will not just recover, it will thrive, providing a haven for threatened species and a place where the community can witness resilience firsthand.
Your support can help to fund nurseries, buy local seed, and put tools in the hands of volunteers across landscapes in need across Australia.

By signing up as a monthly donor, you’ll be helping us restore and protect habitats and landscapes all year round. Your ongoing support ensures seedlings get planted, cared for, and nurtured into thriving woodlands that provide vital habitat for threatened species
Together, we can ensure Charleston’s story is one of recovery, resilience, and renewal.

title: Fire Wise Project Impact
standfirst: The Fire Wise project launched in 2023 with a clear mission: to transform how communities prepare for bushfires by using nature as a partner, not a casualty. Residents, councils, Traditional Owners, and scientists have come together to learn, plant, and build resilience that will last beyond a single fire season.
description: The Fire Wise project launched in 2023 with a clear mission: to transform how communities prepare for bushfires by using nature as a partner, not a casualty.

flow.p: The Fire Wise project launched in 2023 with a clear mission: to transform how communities prepare for bushfires by using nature as a partner, not a casualty. Residents, councils, Traditional Owners, and scientists have come together to learn, plant, and build resilience that will last beyond a single fire season.

Now, as this phase of the project concludes, its impact is clear. Thousands of native, low-flammability plants have been established, seed banks strengthened, and communities equipped with the skills and confidence to continue this work. Fire Wise has shown that protecting homes and landscapes does not have to come at the cost of biodiversity. It can build safer, stronger, and more connected communities ready to face future challenges.
We partnered with 14 groups, uniting councils, local organisations, Traditional Owners, and scientists to bring Fire Wise to communities across South Australia, Victoria, and New South Wales.
With support from FNPW, the Fire Wise project has delivered real, lasting change in how communities prepare for bushfires while supporting biodiversity.

flow.h: Why native planting is part of fire safety

flow.p: Native vegetation is often cleared under the belief it fuels bushfires, leading to biodiversity and habitat loss. However, many native plants, when used strategically, can help reduce fire spread, retain ground moisture, block radiant heat, slow winds, and filter embers.

Fire Wise demonstrates that protecting lives and homes can go hand-in-hand with supporting biodiversity and healthy landscapes. Instead of viewing nature as a threat, Fire Wise positions it as a key ally in bushfire preparedness.

blocks.alt: Volunteers planting in field. People in workshops

flow.p: Fire Wise plants are less likely to ignite, don’t produce embers easily, and retain moisture, which can slow fire spread. In addition, some may smoulder or give off steam instead of burning immediately, reducing fuel for advancing fires.
Examples include:

ul: Sea Berry Saltbush (Rhagodia candolleana)
Tree Hakea (Hakea eriantha)
Boobialla (Myoporum insulare)
Lilly Pilly (Acmena smithii)
Kidney Weed (Dichondra repens)

flow.p: Note: No plant is fireproof, but the right species in the right place can reduce risks and buy critical time in a fire event.
Our Partner, South Gippsland Landcare Network, designed their Fire Wise demonstration sites using layered, strategic “green fire walls” inspired by the Lakes Entrance Landcare guide.

Plant spacing is planned to prevent fires from climbing into canopies while supporting healthy landscapes. Additionally, low-growing, Fire Wise species are positioned near buildings, with trees set further back, while paths, lawns, and gravel breaks are used to separate planting areas. This careful design helps slow fire movement and adds extra protection around homes while maintaining a biodiverse environment.

Fire Wise uses suppression planting with local, low-flammability species. Botanists and Traditional Owners collaborate to create region-specific plant lists, ensuring each community plants what will thrive while reducing fire risks and supporting habitat. These plantings create living barriers that slow fire progression and filter embers before they reach homes.
Fire Wise empowers communities to:

ul: Research and select low-flammability native species
Collect and propagate local seed
Establish revegetation projects on public and private land
Build local seed banks for future resilience

flow.p: Living seed banks and demonstration gardens showcase effective Fire Wise planting, illustrating how design, layering, and maintenance reduce risk while supporting biodiversity.
Fire Wise has strengthened 12 community nurseries to grow and supply local Fire Wise plants, ensuring communities can access the species needed for ongoing resilience.
The Mount Barker Fire Wise demonstration site

blocks.alt: Native plants Fire Wise demonstration site Mount Barker Adelaide

flow.p: After the 2019–2020 Black Summer bushfires, many communities were hesitant to replant, fearing native plants would increase fire risk. Fire Wise provided practical knowledge showing that strategic planting reduces risk and can be part of every fire plan.

Clearing land often creates open pathways for wind and embers, increasing fire spread. By contrast, a moderately dense canopy of native vegetation retains soil moisture, blocks radiant heat, and slows wind, creating a protective buffer around homes and infrastructure.

Fire Wise is not just about fire prevention. By reintroducing fire-resistant native species to stabilise soil, prevent erosion, and support natural regeneration, the project helps communities recover after bushfires while building resilience for future seasons.
This work is especially important where communities and natural environments intersect, protecting people, homes, and biodiversity.
The strength of Fire Wise lies in its collaboration with:

ul: Fire science organisations for evidence-based practices
Local ecologists and botanists for region-specific plant selection
Fire services to align community action with emergency planning
Landcare and Indigenous communities to integrate cultural knowledge and stewardship

flow.p: Fire Wise has proven that fire safety and biodiversity can thrive together. As bushfire risks continue to grow, nature-based, community-led solutions are more important than ever. By engaging communities in planting, learning, and using cultural knowledge, Fire Wise is helping people prepare for and adapt to a changing fire landscape.

blocks.alt: Community volunteers in field
blocks.caption: Panboola Wetlands planting and nursery volunteers

ul: Visit the Alexandrina Community Nursery on Fridays to purchase Fire Wise plants or learn more about Fire Wise gardening. Location: Kessell Road, Goolwa (near the Alexandrina Council Depot).
Volunteer by getting in touch with us, and we can find your nearest nursery.
Visit the demonstration garden at the Environmental Services Centre precinct (100 Springs Road, Mount Barker), next to the community native nursery, open every Thursday.
Explore the Fire Wise Learning Hub for resources to help your community continue building resilience.

title: Land Restoration in South Australia: The Forktree Project Story
standfirst: On a windswept hillside overlooking South Australia’s Fleurieu Peninsula, a remarkable transformation is underway. What was once a degraded paddock, stripped of trees and riddled with weeds, is being patiently restored into living habitat for native wildlife. This is The Forktree Project – a grassroots rewilding and land restoration Australian initiative in Australia led by environmental scientist and explorer Tim Jarvis AM.
description: On a windswept hillside overlooking South Australia’s Fleurieu Peninsula, a remarkable transformation is underway.

flow.p: On a windswept hillside overlooking South Australia’s Fleurieu Peninsula, a remarkable transformation is underway. What was once a degraded paddock, stripped of trees and riddled with weeds, is being patiently restored into living habitat for native wildlife. This is The Forktree Project – a grassroots rewilding and land restoration Australian initiative in Australia led by environmental scientist and explorer Tim Jarvis AM.

Forktree’s story begins in 2019, when Tim purchased the 54-hectare property near Carrickalinga. The land bore all the hallmarks of hard use: cleared for grazing, scarred by dumping, its soils fragile and depleted. Many might have walked away, but Tim saw something else. He saw an opportunity to restore an entire landscape, to prove what could be achieved when science, community, and sheer determination came together.

Today, Forktree is alive with activity. Volunteers and staff are planting native trees and shrubs, trialling new methods of land and water management, and building the foundations of a future forest that will support threatened species and store tens of thousands of tonnes of carbon. What started as a single property has become a beacon for land restoration across Australia.

blocks.alt: rewiring and planting to restore australia land

flow.p: The Forktree Project’s mission is ambitious but clear: rebuild a functioning ecosystem where native plants and animals can thrive once more. The property sits within the broader Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island biodiversity hotspot, a region rich with species found nowhere else. By restoring this land, Forktree is reconnecting habitat that supports nearby reserves including Deep Creek Conservation Park, Myponga Conservation Park, Newland Head, Coorong, and Granite Island.

The work spans several landscapes, coastal heathlands, mallee scrub, wetlands, and grassy woodlands, each with their own ecological role. Among the threatened communities being revived are the Swamps of the Fleurieu Peninsula and Peppermint Box grassy woodlands, both critical for species survival.
The results are already visible: thousands of seedlings in the ground, invasive weeds cleared, soil health improving, and wildlife beginning to return. But this is only the beginning.

flow.h: A Hub for Innovation and Learning

flow.p: Forktree is also a testbed for innovation in ecological restoration. The team has been experimenting with smart irrigation systems linked to soil-moisture sensors, trialling ways to re-establish native grasslands, and developing carbon-estimation methods that could be used by small landholders across the country.

Education is another pillar. Local schools, community groups, and universities use the site as a living classroom, learning about biodiversity, sustainability, and teamwork while getting their hands dirty. Plans for a sustainability centre will further expand these opportunities, creating a permanent space for workshops and wellbeing programs.
This blending of science, education, and community makes Forktree a rare kind of project – one that focuses on land restoration in Australia while also inspiring people.

blocks.alt: volunteers restoring land in South Australia forktree project

flow.p: Every week, volunteers arrive to help shape the future of Forktree. They plant, weed, harvest seed, mend fences, wash pots, and build the infrastructure that keeps the nursery running. The work is varied, sometimes muddy, often tiring, but always deeply rewarding.

Corporate teams are also stepping up. Companies have spent days on site planting trees, sorting tubes, and building fences. For many, it’s a first taste of hands-on conservation and a chance to connect with each other in a new way. Hotels and businesses have joined in too, with creative initiatives like Hotels For Trees, where guests at Mount Lofty House can fund plantings through small acts of sustainability during their stay.
These partnerships reflect a simple truth: restoration at scale requires many hands. At Forktree, every hand makes a difference.

blocks.alt: land restore project south australia

flow.p: The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) is proud to partner with The Forktree Project through our Landscape Resilience Program. In late 2023, we funded the development of a rare seed orchard on site, a secure, vermin-proof 1.5-hectare area dedicated to growing threatened and culturally significant species.

The orchard is designed to safeguard rare plants, provide a steady supply of seed for restoration projects, and act as a living insurance population in the wild. Raised seed beds, expanded irrigation systems, and new infrastructure ensure these species have the best chance to thrive. Importantly, the project also involves Ngarrindjeri land managers, who are being trained to help run the facilities and carry forward cultural and ecological knowledge.

Through this partnership, Forktree’s nursery capacity is growing to 40,000–50,000 plants each year, an extraordinary contribution to South Australia’s restoration needs. These seedlings and seeds won’t just benefit the Fleurieu Peninsula; they will help restore landscapes across the region, linking fragmented habitats and supporting threatened wildlife.

flow.h: Why Forktree Matters for Australia’s Biodiversity

flow.p: FNPW’s vision is to protect and restore biodiversity across Australia, and our support of Forktree reflects that strategy in action. Australia faces an acute shortage of native seed and plants for large-scale restoration. Projects like Forktree’s seed orchard help fill that gap, ensuring that local, genetically appropriate species are available for years to come.

Forktree also demonstrates the power of community-driven conservation. By engaging volunteers, schools, and corporate teams, it builds not only habitat but also public understanding and commitment to biodiversity. That social impact is just as important as the ecological one.

And perhaps most importantly, Forktree provides a model of resilience. In a time of climate uncertainty, it shows how degraded land can be turned into a carbon sink, a wildlife refuge, and a place of learning and wellbeing.

flow.h: Looking Ahead: The Future of Land Restoration in Australia

blocks.alt: land restoration project in australia

flow.p: The Forktree Project is still young, but its trajectory is clear. With every seedling planted, every fence repaired, and every volunteer day completed, it edges closer to restoring a flourishing landscape.

For Tim Jarvis and his team, Forktree is both a personal mission and a public one, a demonstration that ecological decline is not inevitable, and that with vision and collaboration, we can bring nature back.

For FNPW, partnering with Forktree is part of our commitment to help projects across Australia restore landscapes, recover species, and heal Country. Together, we are building the foundations of a more resilient, more biodiverse future.
If you’d like to support Forktree’s work and join a volunteer day, or contribute to FNPW’s national restoration efforts, visit https://fnpw.org.au/corporate-volunteering/ to learn more.

Projects like Forktree are part of a bigger mission to restore Australia’s landscapes, protect threatened species, and heal Country. Your support helps us grow rare plants, train land managers, fund seed banks, and back the grassroots work happening across the country.

to support restoration projects like Forktree and help restore Australia, one landscape at a time.

title: Southern Flinders Ranges: Where Ancient Landscapes Meet Living Culture
standfirst: Rising from the rolling plains of South Australia, the Southern Flinders Ranges is a place where ancient geology, rich biodiversity, and deep cultural heritage come together.
hero_alt: remarkable southern flinders ranges
description: Rising from the rolling plains of South Australia, the Southern Flinders Ranges is a place where ancient geology, rich biodiversity, and deep cultural heritage come together.

flow.p: Rising from the rolling plains of South Australia, the Southern Flinders Ranges is a place where ancient geology, rich biodiversity, and deep cultural heritage come together. Over hundreds of millions of years, wind, water, and shifting earth have carved a dramatic landscape of rugged ridges, deep gorges, and sweeping valleys. Today, these ranges are far more than a scenic backdrop. They are a biodiversity stronghold, a cultural treasure for First Nations peoples, and a natural refuge for plants and animals that have adapted to life in a challenging environment.

flow.h: Why the Southern Flinders Ranges Matters for Biodiversity

blocks.alt: tree, outback, southern flinders ranges mountains

flow.p: The Southern Flinders Ranges holds a unique position in South Australia’s conservation landscape. Here, semi-arid and temperate ecosystems overlap, creating a rare blend of habitats that can support an impressive diversity of species. Many of these plants and animals are endemic, found nowhere else in the world.

This area also acts as a climate refuge, offering shelter and food in a region where rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns are placing increasing pressure on wildlife. The ranges are also of immense geological importance, with rock formations preserving some of the oldest evidence of complex life on Earth.

flow.h: Flora of the Southern Flinders Ranges

flow.p: The vegetation here reflects the adaptability of life in a landscape of extremes. Ridge tops are dominated by sugar gums, cypress pines, and black oak woodlands. In sheltered gullies, you can find grevilleas, lilies, and ferns, while wildflowers burst into bloom after rainfall, carpeting the hillsides in colour.

The endangered Flinders Fingers orchid (Caladenia xantholeuca) is one of the region’s botanical treasures, found nowhere else, while wattles and native grasses help stabilise soil and provide food and habitat for wildlife.

flow.h: Wildlife of the Southern Flinders Ranges

blocks.alt: Western quoll, Wedge-tailed Eagle, emu

flow.p: The Southern Flinders is home to an extraordinary range of animals, from kangaroos and emus to smaller but equally vital species such as dunnarts, planigales, and the cryptic streambank froglet. The Yellow-footed Rock-wallaby, with its distinctive banded tail and golden limbs, has made a strong comeback through focused conservation work.

Predator-proofing and reintroduction programs have brought species like the western quoll (Idnya) and brushtail possum (Virlda) back to the region after decades of absence. Reptiles, including goannas, dragons, and the once-vulnerable Flinders Ranges worm-lizard, add to the diversity, alongside a wealth of birdlife such as wedge-tailed eagles, parrots, and honeyeaters.

flow.h: Cultural Significance to First Nations Peoples

flow.p: The Wapma Thura–Southern Flinders Ranges National Park is the Country of the Nukunu people, whose ancestral connections stretch back tens of thousands of years. “Wapma Thura” means “Snake People” in Nukunu language, a reference to an important creation story.

Today, the park is co-managed with Nukunu Traditional Owners, ensuring that cultural knowledge and practices are embedded in land management. This partnership protects not only the ecological values of the ranges but also the cultural heritage that has shaped them for millennia.

Like much of South Australia, the Southern Flinders Ranges faces the growing impacts of climate change. Prolonged droughts have reduced water availability, stressed vegetation, and increased competition for resources among wildlife. Reduced soil moisture makes it harder for plant communities to recover, leaving landscapes more vulnerable to erosion.

Bushfires are another serious threat. Hotter, drier conditions have increased both the frequency and intensity of fires in the region. Fire can devastate habitat in a matter of hours, destroying food sources and shelter for threatened species, with recovery taking years or even decades in some areas.

blocks.alt: Southern flinders range mountain

flow.p: The Remarkable Southern Flinders Project is a $10 million initiative designed to connect and protect the landscapes of the Southern Flinders. It has united previously separate reserves, including Telowie Gorge, Wirrabara Range, Spaniards Gully, and part of Mount Remarkable National Park, into one continuous conservation area.

This project is about more than protecting land. It creates a world-class nature-based tourism destination with mountain-bike trails, hiking routes, and visitor facilities that encourage people to experience the region while respecting its ecological limits.

Our role in the project includes supporting habitat restoration, improving visitor infrastructure, and working closely with Traditional Owners to ensure cultural and environmental values remain at the heart of all activities.

Standing on a ridge in the Southern Flinders, you might see a wedge-tailed eagle circling overhead or hear the rustle of a rock-wallaby among the cliffs. In spring, orchids and wattles bloom in abundance. At night, quolls and possums emerge under the southern stars, continuing the cycles of life that have unfolded here for countless generations.

The Southern Flinders Ranges is a living system, an ancient geological wonder, and a cultural landscape that holds the stories of the First Nations people who have cared for it for millennia. Protecting it means safeguarding biodiversity, respecting cultural heritage, and ensuring that future generations can connect with its beauty and significance.

Your donation can support projects that restore habitats, protect wildlife, and strengthen cultural stewardship in special places like the Southern Flinders Ranges. Together, we can help safeguard Australia’s unique landscapes and the species that depend on them.
Donate today and be part of creating a healthier, more resilient future for people, wildlife, and Country.

title: Restoring the Grossmans Block: Breathing Life Back into the Southern Flinders
standfirst: In the heart of South Australia, the Southern Flinders stretch from Beetaloo to Wilmington. It is a landscape of rugged peaks, winding gorges, and ancient woodlands. More than scenery, this region is alive with rare plants, unique animals, rich cultural heritage, and a growing tourism economy shaped by nature.
description: In the heart of South Australia, the Southern Flinders stretch from Beetaloo to Wilmington. It is a landscape of rugged peaks, winding gorges, and ancient woodlands.

flow.p: In the heart of South Australia, the Southern Flinders stretch from Beetaloo to Wilmington. It is a landscape of rugged peaks, winding gorges, and ancient woodlands. More than scenery, this region is alive with rare plants, unique animals, rich cultural heritage, and a growing tourism economy shaped by nature.

One of the newest pieces of this living puzzle is the Grossmans Block – 434 hectares now protected as part of the Southern Flinders Precinct Park Complex. Securing this land is a vital step in stitching the region’s ecosystems back together.

For decades, Grossmans was worn down by grazing and cropping. Native plants were trampled, waterholes disturbed, and fragile soils left exposed. The damage spread beyond the property, fragmenting habitats and putting vulnerable species at risk.
Now that the land is under protection, those pressures have been lifted. The difference is already clear:

ul: 13 rare plant species are safeguarded.
9 conservation-listed animals now have secure habitat.
The nationally significant Flinders Worm-lizard has a protected refuge.

flow.p: The transformation has already begun. With stock removed, weeds controlled, and careful management in place, Grossmans is shifting from a degraded paddock to a thriving refuge. Looking ahead, the goal is to scale up restoration, expand habitat corridors, and strengthen First Nations partnerships across the region.
This is not just one patch of land saved. It is a critical link in restoring ecological connections across the Southern Flinders.

Grossmans is a patchwork of ecosystems. River Red Gums shade the creeks, rocky ridges hold native grasses and Yakka, and Blue Gum and Sheoak woodlands provide shelter for birds, reptiles, and small mammals. Even areas scarred by fire or grazing still hold the seeds of renewal.
These ecosystems include:

ul: River Red Gum creek lines, once overgrazed, now offering nesting space for woodland birds and shelter for reptiles.
Blue Gum woodlands, beginning to rebound, providing food for small marsupials and pollinators.
Sheoak and Blue Gum woodlands, among the most intact areas, rich with insects that sustain species like the diamond firetail.
Open Blue Gum woodland, degraded but with strong potential to recover as habitat for the Flinders Worm-lizard.
Mallee pockets, small in size yet vital for ground-dwelling fauna and nectar-feeding insects.
Burnt Blue Gum and Sugar Gum woodland, recovering since the 2014 Bangor Fire, now offering food and perches for wedge-tailed eagles.
Exotic grasslands, still dominated by non-native species, but with grazing removed they can regenerate into native habitat for small mammals and ground-nesting birds.

flow.p: A Bushland Assessment in 2022 confirmed the importance of this diversity, identifying seven vegetation types and awarding the site 2,724.95 SEB (Significant Environmental Benefit) points. In simple terms, Grossmans is among the most valuable conservation land in the region. With grazing gone and good rains ahead, many of these areas will bounce back quickly, creating fresh shelter and food for wildlife.
On the map, Grossmans sits beside Beetaloo Reservoir and on the edge of the newly created Wapma Thura–Southern Flinders Ranges National Park. Protecting this land:

ul: Closes gaps in habitat corridors.
Links creek lines, woodlands, and ridges into one connected system.
Places the block under the same protections as the wider park.

flow.p: Strategic acquisitions like this do more than save individual sites. They turn scattered fragments into functioning landscapes.
Securing Grossmans was only possible through strong partnerships and major investment.

The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife contributed, enabling the Department for Environment and Water (DEW) to purchase the property. Covering 496.51 hectares across four parcels, the block is now protected under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1972 and will be managed by DEW for at least the next decade.

This project came to life thanks to the combined efforts of governments, councils, local organisations, and the Nukunu Wapma Thura Aboriginal Corporation. Together, they are shaping the Southern Flinders into a conservation stronghold and a destination for people who love nature.
Key partners include:

ul: The South Australian and Australian Governments
Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife
Northern Areas Council
District Council of Mount Remarkable
Port Pirie Regional Council
Regional Development Australia Yorke and Mid-North
Nukunu Wapma Thura Aboriginal Corporation

flow.p: Securing Grossmans was just the beginning. Real restoration takes patience, monitoring, and ongoing resources. You can play a part:

ul: Donate to support weed control, habitat recovery, and species surveys.
Become a monthly donor to provide steady, reliable support.
Spread the word so more people know why this land matters.

flow.p: Every action helps turn Grossmans into a cornerstone of a thriving Southern Flinders Precinct.

title: Students release turtle hatchlings in a conservation first
standfirst: It starts with curious minds, a walk to the wetlands, and a turtle in hand.
hero_alt: A student holding a freshwater turtle hatchling at the wetland edge.
description: Students from PLC Sydney released eastern long-necked turtle hatchlings they had incubated for five weeks, a first for the Turtles in Schools program supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife.

flow.p: It starts with curious minds, a walk to the wetlands, and a turtle in hand.

On Tuesday morning, students from Presbyterian Ladies’ College (PLC) Sydney gathered under the late-summer sun at Oatlands Golf Course to release eastern long-necked turtle hatchlings into the wild—hatchlings they had incubated, monitored, and cared for over the past five weeks.

This was no ordinary field trip. It was the culmination of months of learning, nurturing, and hands-on science. But more importantly, it marked a real-world environmental impact: where science class became species recovery, and students became conservationists.

The event is part of Turtles in Schools, a national education and conservation program supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) and delivered through the 1 Million Turtles Project, led by Professor Ricky Spencer of Western Sydney University. A long-time champion of citizen science and student-led conservation, Professor Spencer has helped shape programs that turn local communities into active conservation partners.

blocks.alt: PLC students release freshwater turtle into the wild

flow.p: Freshwater turtles across Australia are disappearing—largely unnoticed. In some regions, their populations have collapsed by over 90%. Foxes destroy most nests. Wetland habitat is vanishing. Climate change and disease are adding pressure.
These animals are far from ornamental. They recycle nutrients, control algae, and help keep rivers clean. When turtles decline, the health of our wetlands begins to break down.

In November, PLC students worked alongside scientists and Oatlands Golf Course staff to relocate two vulnerable clutches of turtle eggs. The eggs were incubated in a simple, school-based setup, maintained daily by students. The goal: protect them from predation and give them the best chance at survival. Five weeks later, every egg hatched.
On release day, students gently returned the hatchlings—now bright-eyed, alert, and strong—to the wetland where they were originally found.
Professor Spencer called it “education at its most powerful.”

“It’s a great opportunity for schools to demonstrate that they can be a major part of conservation outcomes.” Said Professor Spencer. “It’s a combination of community conservation in action. This is the first school that’s ever done this and really doing what zoos and wildlife parks do—raising turtles from eggs to this release point as hatchlings”.

blocks.alt: PLC sydney students at Oatlands Golf Course Wetlands

flow.p: Turtles in Schools works because it turns abstract environmental issues into something tangible and personal. Students aren’t just learning—they’re contributing to real species recovery.

CEO of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, Ian Darbyshire, said “What we’re hoping is this is the first of many, many, many future releases where we create a sustainable program of protecting the turtles of the Murray-Darling Basin by getting schools to do this every year forever, so that we can protect the population of turtles.”
He added, “The turtles were laid on the floating islands that Ricky Spencer has created in part of the sponsorship with the Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife.”

More schools are now introducing “hatchling hubs” into their classrooms, where students incubate eggs, monitor local wetlands, test water quality, and log turtle sightings through the national TurtleSAT platform.

flow.h: A National Effort with Real Impact

flow.p: Turtles in Schools is one part of the broader 1 Million Turtles Project—a national collaboration uniting researchers, educators, governments, and communities.
Partners include:

ul: Leading universities: Western Sydney, La Trobe, Sydney, Murdoch, New England, and Ohio University
Conservation groups: FNPW, Aussie Ark, WIRES, and Turtle Rescues NSW
Government agencies and local councils
Schools and community groups—beginning with the pioneering efforts of PLC Sydney

blocks.alt: PLC students, Ricky Spencer and Ian Darbyshire FNPW

flow.h: A Scalable Model for the Future

flow.p: At FNPW, we believe conservation is most effective when it’s hands-on, local, and connected to the next generation. Young people, with the right support, can lead real environmental change.
Every turtle released this week was one that wouldn’t have survived without intervention. And every student involved walked away with a deeper understanding of nature—and their power to protect it.

Turtles in Schools is more than a classroom initiative—it’s a scalable, national model for conservation education. And it’s proof that the next generation doesn’t have to wait to make a difference—they’re already leading it.
Discover more projects like this one and explore how you can be part of protecting Australia’s wildlife. Contact us.

To deliver maximum impact and ensure that we’re funding priority projects which are pivotal in safeguarding and preserving Australia’s rich natural biodiversity, we align with international and national environmental objectives, including:

The Kunming-Montreal Global Diversity Framework(GBF) (Targets 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8). United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals(Goals 13, 15 and 17). International extinction priorities via the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Australia’s EPBC Act List of Threatened Species alongside state listings. Since COP 15, our efforts have echoed the worldwide push for conservation. We’re dedicated to goals like protecting 30% of land and marine areas by 2030 and preserving Indigenous knowledge. Our partnerships extend to biodiversity reporting frameworks, guiding our investments for maximum environmental benefit. By expanding national parks, saving threatened species and restoring our land, we’re building a sustainable future for Australia. Some of the key highlights from our report:

Growing Parks  Supported 50+ land purchases since 1970. Developing the Wapma Thura Southern Flinders Ranges National Park, a world-class nature tourism destination. Expanding the UNESCO World Heritage Listed Gondwana Rainforests.   Saving Species Work alongside governments to prioritise the protection of threatened native species. Supporting 167 threatened plant and animal species across Australia. The Wildlife Heroes project aided over 700 species over three years, with over 50% being threatened mammals. Working to save 1 million turtles in the Murray-Darling Basin.   Healing Our Land Planting over 700,000 native trees for restoration. Building one of Australia’s largest community-led restoration projects across 4 states enabled by 19 local community nurseries and 10,000+ volunteers. The Fire Wise project, launched with CSIRO, is a catalyst for community engagement in best-practice bushfire risk mitigation, ensuring a safer and ecologically vibrant future. Collaborating with Indigenous groups to create projects grounded in a blend of Indigenous knowledge and scientific evidence.   Thank you. Together we will continue to create meaningful and lasting impact.   Happy Impact Reading!

flow.p: Hosted by: Vincent Turner

David Goldman is a seasoned professional in the field of environmental conservation, and a representative of the Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife in Australia. With a dedication to the preservation of national parks and wildlife, David brings a wealth of insight into biodiversity and land management. Based in Sydney, Australia, his role involves collaborative efforts to expand the reach and protection of natural reserves across the country, aiming to save threatened species and enhance ecological resilience.

In this engaging episode of Shape the System, host Vincent interviews David Goldman from the Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife. Together, they delve into the pressing issues surrounding biodiversity, wildlife preservation, and ecosystem resilience in Australia. They discuss innovative ways of safeguarding natural habitats and the pivotal role of land conservation in maintaining a diverse and flourishing biosphere.

David sheds light on the foundation’s key projects, including the pursuit of enlarging national parks and establishing green corridors. He highlights the importance of eliminating invasive species to allow native flora and fauna to thrive, and the role of community participation in protecting and revitalizing the environment. With a comprehensive look at government partnerships and philanthropy, this episode is rich with insights into the tactical steps being taken to meet Australia’s 30×30 conservation commitments.

The conversation further explores the evolution of the foundation, which has transitioned from purely land acquisition to encompassing land regeneration and public engagement through the Backyard Buddies program. They also touch on the economics of land conservation, including engaging with private landholders and the future of sustainable revenue models for environmental charities.

ul: The Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife aims to protect 30% of Australia’s natural land by 2030 by purchasing and regenerating land adjacent to national parks.
Biodiversity preservation has a direct impact on ecological resilience, crucial for combating extreme weather events and climate change.
Efforts include volunteering, community nurseries, and working with local governments to eliminate invasive species and promote native ecosystems.
The concept of ‘Backyard Buddies’ promotes individual action, underscoring the connection between one’s backyard and larger ecological systems.
Innovative models for sustainable futures include leveraging carbon sequestration to fund further land acquisition, demonstrating an evolution from traditional donation-based funding.

flow.p: “The federal government put out a list, continuously update that list. It’s part of the EPBC act, and currently there’s almost 2000 threatened species, both floor and fauna.” – David Goldman
“Often what our work will involve before even handing it over the land over as national park is that revegetation or regeneration of the land.” – David Goldman
“87% of the money that comes to us, we will put it back into the purpose.” – David Goldman
“I personally, and I’m sure there are a number of people at the office, don’t believe that the donor model is necessarily the long-term sustainable future.” – David Goldman
“So it’s about being a bit more clever in how we look at our future and what revenue models we put in place to ensure that we are sustainable.” – David Goldman
No specific resources or references were mentioned in the transcript.

Embark on a journey through the transformative efforts of the Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife by listening to the full episode. Discover the innovative strategies that are shaping the future of Australia’s natural landscapes. Stay tuned for more episodes from Shape the System to be inspired by stories of individuals and organizations redefining how we interact with and protect our planet.

title: Empowering First Nations Women
standfirst: On March 8th, International Women’s Day, we turn our attention to the incredible contributions of women in First Nations ranger programs across West and Central Arnhem Land. These women are not just protecting their land; they’re forging pathways for young women, preserving cultural knowledge, and making significant strides in conservation efforts.
description: On March 8th, International Women’s Day, we turn our attention to the incredible contributions of women in First Nations ranger programs across West and Central Arnhem Land.

flow.p: On March 8th, International Women’s Day, we turn our attention to the incredible contributions of women in First Nations ranger programs across West and Central Arnhem Land. These women are not just protecting their land; they’re forging pathways for young women, preserving cultural knowledge, and making significant strides in conservation efforts.

Arnhem Land stands as a bastion of biodiversity and cultural heritage, and the stewardship of this land traditionally fell into the hands of men. However, the inclusion of women in ranger programs is revolutionising conservation efforts. Women bring with them a wealth of ecological knowledge passed down through generations, essential for the preservation of habitats and species. Their engagement on Country is not just crucial; it’s indispensable for the survival of traditional ecological wisdom.

blocks.caption: Photo by Karrkad Kanjdji

flow.h: The Impact of Ranger Programs on First Nations Communities

flow.p: The Warddeken and Mimal Women’s Ranger Programs exemplify this commitment to inclusivity and sustainability. These programs provide women with flexible, culturally appropriate opportunities, enriching their lives while safeguarding their heritage. Through consultation with Traditional Owners, these programs have expanded, fostering equality and broadening the scope of conservation work.
Lorraine Namarnyilk, a Daluk (Women’s) Ranger, beautifully encapsulates the spirit of these initiatives:

“Women together is a good way to work. Sometimes we mix it up with the men but when we work together, we have a lot of fun – we talk about culture, our family, the Country we work in and our relationship to it. I love working as a ranger because of the different opportunities to do all kinds of work that helps keep the Country healthy. This is the best job that I’ve had, and I want to keep learning more and getting more work done.”

blocks.caption: Photo by Karrkad Kanjdji Trust

flow.h: Supporting First Nations Women in Conservation

flow.p: The Warddeken Daluk (Women’s) Ranger Program, supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW), is leading the charge in this movement. Through projects like the Mayh (animals) Recovery Project, Warddeken Rangers are employing their expertise to protect and enhance their 1.4-million-hectare Indigenous Protected Area (IPA).

Karrkad Kanjdji Trust (KKT) plays a pivotal role in supporting women rangers across the region. Recognising the entrenched gender inequalities, KKT has spearheaded efforts to amplify the voices and roles of women in ranger workforces. These initiatives have seen remarkable success, with women now comprising a significant portion of the ranger workforce.

ul: Around 50% of Mimal’s workforce are women, equating to 36 women in 2023 who participated in 16 different training and education courses.
Around 74 women are employed by Warddeken on average each quarter, who worked a combined 13,000 hours in 2023. This is around 45% of Warddeken’s workforce.

blocks.caption: Photo by Karrkad Kanjdji Trust

flow.p: The journey doesn’t end here. The Strong Women for Healthy Country Network (SWHCN) represents the next chapter in this narrative. Born out of a desire for solidarity and support, this network unites First Nations women from across the Northern Territory, advocating for their rights and well-being and striving to become an independent organisation providing wrap-around support for women’s wellbeing and health, leadership, and land management capabilities.

As we celebrate International Women’s Day, let us recognise and honour the resilience, wisdom, and leadership of Indigenous women in ranger programs. Theirs is a legacy of stewardship and empowerment, shaping not just the land but also the future of conservation.

description: The Green Gully tree planting project faced logistical challenges due to site access and terrain, yet received enthusiastic support from our team members.

flow.p: The Green Gully tree planting project faced logistical challenges due to site access and terrain, yet received enthusiastic support from our team members. The initiative was embraced with dedication, with many expressing interest in continuing the area’s rehabilitation. Our approach comprised two phases: initially, we focused on removing old fencing and damaged infrastructure to reduce wildlife entrapment and environmental impact.
Our project aims was to address regrowth weeds and conduct thorough site preparation before replanting the affected areas with native species trees.

This restoration effort was crucial for replacing and repairing the habitat corridor that was lost in previous fires. The impact of this endeavor extended beyond ecological restoration as it directly benefits a diverse range of native mammals that inhabit the region.

Among these are koalas, eastern pygmy-possums, yellow-bellied gliders, squirrel gliders, feathertail gliders, brushtail possums, greater gliders, sugar gliders, short-beaked echidnas, platypuses, bandicoots, common wombats, common wallaroos, brush-tailed rock wallabies, spotted-tailed quolls, swamp wallabies, red-necked wallabies, and Eastern Grey Kangaroos.
By supporting the needs of these park dwellers, our replanting efforts contribute to land stabilisation and foster a healthier ecosystem for both wildlife and the surrounding environment.

title: Growing Koala Trees
standfirst: Australia’s iconic Koala is facing a dire situation due to habitat loss, fragmentation, and degradation. The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) is stepping in to help reverse this trend through innovative habitat restoration efforts that focus on growing native koala food trees.
description: Australia’s iconic Koala is facing a dire situation due to habitat loss, fragmentation, and degradation.

flow.p: Australia’s iconic Koala is facing a dire situation due to habitat loss, fragmentation, and degradation. The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) is stepping in to help reverse this trend through innovative habitat restoration efforts that focus on growing native koala food trees.
DOWNLOAD THE infographic

What’s the Importance of Native Koala Food Trees?  Koalas, listed as endangered under the national Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation (EPBC) Act, rely heavily on specific eucalyptus species for food. However, habitat loss and changes in land use have led to a shortage of these vital koala food trees, particularly those that are of local provenance and best suited for regional Koala populations. The decline in Koala populations can be directly attributed to the destruction of their habitat, which not only reduces food availability but also fragments their living space, making it harder for them to survive and reproduce.

flow.h: The Community-Based Nursery Growing Koala Native Trees

flow.p: To tackle the shortage of Koala trees, the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife runs the Landscape Resilience Program, which includes 30 Community-Based Nurseries. This initiative engages local plant nurseries, such as the Friends of the Koala Nursery in Lismore, NSW, to grow native plants specifically needed for habitat restoration projects.

Over the past three years, the Friends of the Koala Nursery has produced over 190,000 plants, including key eucalyptus species (Eucalyptus, Corymbia, Angophora) that are preferred by Koalas in the Lismore region. This grassroots approach supports Koala populations and enhances the resilience of the ecosystem.

blocks.caption: Friends of the Koala Community Nursery

flow.h: A Collaborative Effort Creating a Lasting Impact

flow.p: The success of the Community-Based Nursery Program hinges on collaboration with local Landcare groups, government organisations, and volunteers. By providing high-quality, local plants, FNPW and its partners ensure that habitat restoration projects are ecologically appropriate and sustainable.

This approach benefits not just Koalas but also other species that share their habitat, such as the Greater Glider (Petauroides Volans), another nationally threatened species. By fostering a diverse range of native plants, the program helps create a balanced and healthy environment that supports a wide array of wildlife.

blocks.caption: Bloom & Ivy. Photo by Friends of the Koala

flow.p: By focusing on habitat restoration and the growth of native Koala food trees, these efforts provide a solid foundation for the recovery of Koala populations in Australia. As part of the National Recovery Plan for the Koala, continued support for community-based nurseries and habitat restoration initiatives is essential. With ongoing collaboration and dedication, there is hope for a better future where Koalas and other species can thrive in their natural habitats.
